#8521. Two Climbers Missing on Gangapurna West

Hidesuke Taneishi and Tetsu Hashimoto of Japan are missing on unclimbed Gangapurna West in Nepal’s Annapurna region.

The Japanese pair headed to the 7,140m peak in September, and we heard no further news of them. After a major storm hit Nepal’s mountains three weeks ago, we presumed they had retreated. But now it seems they did not. They have been out of touch since October 15, after encountering severe weather conditions during their attempt to climb the peak, According to News on Nepal.

Hidesuke Taneishi, left, and Tetsu Hashimoto, right, with a support team member in Kathmandu earlier this week. Photo: Cosmo Adventure

The Russian team that reached the mountain earlier this month reportedly found no sign of the Japanese climbers on the peak. Bad weather forced the Russians down from their summit attempt at 6,800m.

A helicopter search-and-rescue operation is now underway, Manang Chief District Officer Mukti Prasad Khanal has confirmed. Today, high-altitude helicopters and drones successfully recovered some of their gear, including trekking poles, near 7,050m, but the climbers themselves remain missing.

Gangapurna West is also known as Asapurna or Peak Lachenal.

#8518. Everest West Ridge Thwarts Climbers a Second Time

The three-man Russian team returned to Everest’s West Ridge but found the route even more difficult than they expected. After two days of struggle, they’re heading back to Base Camp.

On October 20, Andrei Vasiliev, Serguey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov went back up to the Lho La and pitched their tent on the wide plateau beyond. They still had time to fix more rope higher up.

“We moved…over terrain we’d already covered on the previous rotation,” the climbers texted to team member Natalya Belyankina, who had to abandon the expedition due to illness.

“The weather is good: sunny, with light winds, but cold,” they noted. “Progress was painfully slow today due to heavy packs and a persistent cough,” the climbers noted later.

On Wednesday, they hoped to reach 7,500m, spend the night there, check the route ahead, and then retreat to the plateau. However, they didn’t get as far as they had planned.

“We didn’t cover much ground today,” leader Andrei Vsiliev texted Anna Piunova of The Mountain Club. “The route is no walk in the park. We have to climb steep snowy slopes that conceal rock sections underneath.”

To make things worse, they found no suitable bivy spots at their highest point, so they had to retreat to a place where they could pitch their tent for the night. Today, they were just too exhausted to keep going.

“We’re heading down; we’re sick and need to recover,” Vasiliev told Belyankina. “We can barely keep moving.”

#8515. Colorado Hiker Creates Ultimate Thru-Hike Across His Home State

Donovan Rice got into thru-hiking almost by accident. Already outdoorsy, he graduated from long hikes to planning to climb all 53 of Colorado’s 14,000’ers (mountains above 14,000 feet, or 4,267m). While researching which peaks required overnight camping, he realized that some people’s hikes just keep going.

“I thought, there’s no way somebody can walk from Mexico to Canada. That’s just ridiculous,” Rice explained. “I fell in love with that idea.”

From there, it was a slippery slope. First came the Pacific Crest Trail (PCT), from the Mexican border in California to the Canadian border in British Columbia. Then he did the Continental Divide Trail (CDT), tracing the Rocky Mountains from New Mexico to the Montana-Canada border. Before he knew it, he had a trail name — Iceman —and was working the gig economy to free up time for wilderness adventures.

But that’s where most people’s slippery slope levels out. Hiking the 4,988km CDT is as meaty a project as most of us can imagine. But for Rice, it only opened the floodgates. He was fascinated by everything that didn’t make it into famous routes, especially the ridges and mountains he passed in his home state of Colorado that were just off trail.

“There’s all this stuff the CDT doesn’t hit because it is following the Continental Divide,” he told ExplorersWeb. “So when I got to the end of the Colorado section, about 700 miles, I was thinking, man, if there were a 2,000-mile version of that, it would be my dream thru-hike. Just that non-stop, relentless brutality that is Colorado.”

Colorado has 14,000′ peaks but also deserts. Photo: Donovan Rice

Rice started thinking about a massive thru-hike loop of the state. His idea was to stitch together existing trails and form new ones where necessary.

“I dropped a load of pins across the areas in Colorado I wanted to visit, then I pulled out a public lands layer of the map to see how I might connect the areas,” he explained. “The three core design philosophies were beauty, breadth, and epicness. I wanted to see beautiful views, I wanted to cover as much of Colorado’s diversity as possible, and I wanted to take the most iconic and epic route possible.”

Unlike places like the UK, there is no “right to roam” in Colorado, so connecting the route to avoid private land was tricky. Occasionally, he had to link bits of public land and sections of trail in the “least worst way,” with short road walks when private property appeared to halt progress.

As he tacked on mountain peaks and the national parks he wanted to explore, his route swelled to a monstrous 3,000km+. His itinerary now included all 11 of Colorado’s national forests, three of its national parks, 13 14,000’ers and 47 13,000’ers.

“This is not an efficient route,” Rice admits. “You could walk the full perimeter of Colorado and then hike the Colorado Trail [an existing 885km trail from Waterton Canyon near Denver to Durango], and then still have kilometers left over [to complete the loop].”

The Great Colorado Route. Photo: Donovan Rice

The route looked epic on paper, but Rice still needed to prove it could actually be thru-hiked. After months of planning, Rice set off on his Great Colorado Route from Gunnison National Park on May 14, 2026. He traveled ultra-light, carrying just six kilos of gear, with just a quilt instead of a sleeping bag and a tarp rather than a tent.

“I wanted it to be lightweight enough that I could be nimble on the mountains while doing these technical traverses,” said Rice. Traveling light was wise. Rice’s Great Colorado Route is challenging, with plenty of scrambling and sustained time at altitude.

“The crux might be between Bailey and Rocky Mountain National Park. You go over the Mount Evans Wilderness, two 14,000’ers, hop on the Front Range across several 13,000’ers, and then across the Tenmile Range, and then the absolutely brutal Gore Range.”

Rice spent 141 days tramping his trail, eventually finishing on October 1 after 3,252km. While he describes the route as “definitely not beginner-friendly” — due to plenty of cross-country terrain, off-trail navigation, and route-finding — it doesn’t require mountaineering skills.

“For me, the real sweet spot is Class three scrambling,” he says. “Once you get up to Class four, it starts getting really scary, and I had no tolerance at all for true Class five rock climbing.”

However, he did pack an ice ax, micro-spikes, snow gaiters, and a lightweight helmet to protect against rockfall. He also made an effort to structure the route to provide relief between the most challenging sections, giving the trail an ebb and flow, and potential hikers time to decompress.

The Ballard to La Junta traverse. Photo: Donovan Rice

Overall, his focus on scenic beauty over contrived difficulty helped keep the route somewhat accessible. This is important because Rice hopes that other hikers will give it a go. He is building a website that maps the route, segment by segment, with GPS coordinates to help future hikers find the best places to camp or alternative paths depending on trail conditions. This is a May-through-October trail, but Rice stresses that it is unrealistic to expect perfect conditions for four and a half months.

“This is one of those routes where bailouts will have to happen,” Rice explained. “You’ll have to take a low route or an alternate. I’m hoping to revisit some of the areas in the future and establish some of these alternative routes.”

He aims to get all 29 segments of the initial route fully mapped on The Great Colorado website by the end of the year. It’s a big project, almost as big as the hike itself.

“I need to see how many people will actually give it a try. People can do segments. I’d love to see more thru-hikers do this, but the big challenge is that I think the majority of thru-hikers will look at this and think ‘that’s above my pay grade’.”

The Castles, Colorado. Photo: Donovan Rice

Once he finishes the website, the level of interest might dictate his next steps. “I don’t know what level of formal recognition I want to try for. Do I want to try to get it codified? Or should it stay unofficial and remain just some cool thing someone did that published information on how to do it yourself.”

Whether or not his Great Colorado Route ever gains the name recognition of the CDT or PCT, Rice has authored something unique, and in a world full of rehashes and copycats, that makes it special.

Rice looking down on Island Lake from Ulysses S. Grant Peak. Photo: Donovan Rice

#8511. Bodies of Missing Japanese Climbers Found on Gangapurna West

This morning, rescuers found the bodies of Japanese climbers Hidesuke Taneishi, 40, and Tetsu Hashimoto, 25, on Gangapurna West.

“Both bodies were found at around 6,300m on the south side of Gangapurna West,” the rescue team told The Tourism Times.

Hidesuke Taneishi (left) and Tetsu Hashimoto (right) with a support team member in Kathmandu earlier this week. Photo: Cosmo Adventure

The climbers were attempting the first ascent of the 7,140m mountain and lost contact on October 15 at approximately 7,050m on their summit push.

A search-and-rescue team has been looking for the pair since October 19. Unfortunately, no one knew where they were on the mountain, or even if they were on the mountain at all. Therefore, the search started at Manang village, with no success.

The team included helicopter pilot Sobit Gauchan, high-altitude photographer and climber Manish Maharjan, and IFMGA mountain guide Pansang Rinzee Sherpa. The helicopter dropped Maharjan and Rinzee at 5,750m, and from there they used a drone to search the upper slopes. They scouted the northeast and southwest sides of the mountain, and finally found the remains of the Japanese climbers’ higher camp. Today, they found the bodies on the south side.

As for the cause of the accident, Rinzee told ExplorersWeb that their observations of the terrain pointed to a snow slab collapse.

Several teams have attempted Gangapurna West, located next to the Annapurna massif in Manang district, since it opened to foreign teams in 2014. However, none have summited. The mountain is also known as Asapurna or Lachenal Peak.

Team leader Hidesuke Taneishi was nominated for a Piolet d’Or last year after his first ascent of 6,652m Pholesobi Peak, also in Nepal, via a direct route up its vertiginous north face with Hiroki Yamamoto.

Hidesuke Taneishi on the summit of Pholesobi Peak. Photo: Hiroki Yamamoto

#8507. Introducing the Banff Mountain Book Competition Winners, 2026

Every year, the Banff Centre Mountain Film and Book Festival celebrates the best mountain and adventure writing, film, and photography. The literary highlight of this alpine-themed celebration is the Banff Mountain Book Competition, with eight categories and one grand prize. The jury will award the grand prize at the festival, but the category winners have been announced.

First, the two Special Jury Mentions. Jack Plant’s Spirit of the Great Bear showcases his spectacular photography of the Great Bear Forest. Meanwhile, Ian Nicholson’s Glacier Travel & Crevasse Rescue: Essential Skills for Snow Travel does exactly what it says on the tin. “Of all the skill sets required for mountain climbing, perhaps none are as intimidating as glacier travel. But with carefully crafted instructions and illustrations, Nicholson takes us behind the curtain,” jury member Lauren DeLaunay Miller explains.

The Mountain Literature award went to Lone Wolf: Walking the Line Between Civilization and Wildness by Adam Weymouth. Weymouth dives into the place of wild animals in modern Europe, a continent “undergoing profound climatic, environmental, and political changes.”

Black Bear: A Story of Siblinghood and Survival by Trina Moyles won the Environmental Literature category. “Black Bear seamlessly weaves together two complex storylines, laying bare Moyles’ relationships with her brother and with the wildlife she meets while working in a fire watch tower in Alberta.”

The Mountain Article prize, awarded to a magazine piece rather than a book, went to The Misfits by Chad Heddleston. Heddleston chose to profile rock climbing couple Jan and Herb Conn. “These two exist in the spirit and austerity of the pioneering European climbers of the early 20th century. The writing highlights their uniqueness and the integrity of their life choices,” jury member David Chambre said.

Pioneering rock climbers Jan and Herb Conn. Photo: Dwight Deal

The Adventure Travel prize went to North to the Future: An Offline Adventure through the Changing Wilds of Alaska by Ben Weissenbach. “Weissenbach — an L.A. native with little prior wilderness experience — treks through the Alaskan tundra with a series of eccentric environmental scientists and returns with a new perspective on technology and a revitalized sense of wonder for the natural world.”

Cabin Wild: Alpine Bivouac Huts by Ben Tibbetts won the Guidebook award. “A captivating volume that invites us to see the Alps in a new light, through an intimate journey around a selection of bivouac huts across Italy, Switzerland, and France,” according to jury member Rob Lovell.

The Mountain Image award went to Fjell: A Faithful Witness by Orsolya Haarberg. “A highly original book that takes us on a journey through the Norwegian highlands. It is as much an art book as a book about mountains,” explains jury member David Chambre.

Finally, The Great Mixed Climbs of Scotland by Guy Robertson & Hamish Frost won the Climbing Literature prize. “The Great Mixed Climbs of Scotland combines stunning photography and evocative essays in a truly spectacular ode to Scottish winter climbing. By profiling important routes through the eyes of the climbers who created them, Guy Robertson and Hamish Frost have created an exceptional book.”

The category-winning authors get cash prizes and a chance to win the grand prize at the festival on November 5.

#8503. The Mountain That Looked Impossible: Muztagh Tower, 1956

For nearly half a century, a single photograph defined one of the Karakoram’s most striking peaks. Taken in 1909 and reproduced in books and journals, it showed Muztagh Tower as a vertical blade, a slender tooth of rock and ice rising from the glaciers with no obvious weakness. Generations of climbers studied it and concluded that the mountain was impossible to summit.

In the summer of 1956, two independent expeditions arrived on opposite sides of the peak, each convinced they were looking at one of the range’s last great unclimbed problems. But the photograph had misled them.

Vittorio Sella was born in 1859 in Biella, Italy, into a family connected to the mountains. His uncle, Quintino Sella, had helped found the Club Alpino Italiano, and his father, Giuseppe Venanzio Sella, was a pioneer of early photography who published the first important Italian treatise on the subject.

Vittorio Sella combined serious alpinism with large-format photography. He made the first winter ascent of the Matterhorn in 1882, followed by the first winter traverse of Mont Blanc. Throughout his career, he carried heavy glass-plate cameras into the high Alps, the Caucasus, Alaska, the Ruwenzori, and the Karakoram.

Sella’s photographic technique was excellent. His plates were large, the detail exceptional, and the compositions carefully chosen. His work was much admired, including by American photographer Ansel Adams. In a 1946 article for the Sierra Club Bulletin, Adams paid tribute to Sella’s work, writing:

“The purity of Sella’s interpretations move the spectator to a religious awe. Sella has brought to us not only the facts and forms of far-off splendours of the world, but the essence of experience which finds a spiritual response in the inner recesses of our mind and heart.”

Vittorio Sella. Photo: Alpine Club Photo Library

Sella’s most important Himalayan photographs came from the 1909 K2 expedition led by Luigi Amedeo, Duke of the Abruzzi.

Filippo De Filippi’s official account of the expedition, Karakoram and Western Himalaya 1909 (published in English in 1912), was illustrated throughout with Sella’s images. Those photographs remain among the finest early records of the range. One of them, a telephoto view of Muztagh Tower, became famous far beyond the expedition report, and inadvertently sparked a legendary mountaineering myth.

Muztagh Tower (7,276m) is located in the Baltoro Muztagh of the Karakoram, on the border between Pakistan’s Gilgit-Baltistan and China’s Xinjiang. It rises between the Baltoro and Sarpo Laggo Glaciers, just north of the main Baltoro corridor leading toward K2.

The peak has two summits only a short distance apart. The eastern peak is the true summit, and the western summit is a few metres lower. From most angles, the mountain is a substantial massif with steep but not uniformly vertical faces. From one particular viewpoint it collapses into something that looks far more extreme.

Muztagh Tower taken from the Upper Baltoro Glacier in 1919 by Vittorio Sella. The tower appears as an impregnable tooth. The photo inspired mountaineers for decades. Photo: Vittorio Sella

Sella took the image of Muztagh Tower from the upper Baltoro Glacier, looking northwest toward the mountain. The twin summits lined up almost perfectly. The long telephoto lens compressed the intervening ground and presented the peak as a narrow, knife-edged tower whose walls appeared to fall nearly vertically from summit to glacier.

From other angles the peak revealed broader ridges and less precipitous slopes, but this single compressed view was the one that circulated widely. The effect was really dramatic, but as later climbers discovered, also misleading. In 1941, Sella’s photo of Muztagh Tower appeared in a mountaineering book under the caption “The Last Citadel.” The image fixed the mountain’s reputation for decades.

Muztagh Tower, 1909. Photo: Vittorio Sella

In 1956, a British team and a French team both set out for Muztagh Tower, drawn in large part by Sella’s photograph.

The British team, led by John Hartog and consisting of Joe Brown, Ian McNaught-Davis, Tom Patey, and liaison officer Captain Riaz Mohammad, chose the Northwest Ridge. They planned to approach via the Muztagh and Chagaran glaciers on the western side of the peak.

The French party, led by Guido Magnone, included Andre Contamine, Paul Keller, Robert Paragot, Francois Florence, and liaison officer Ali Usman. They worked from the eastern side, aiming for what became the eastern arête after reconnaissance ruled out the North Ridge. The two groups operated independently on opposite flanks of the mountain.

The British established Base Camp on the Muztagh Glacier on May 28, 1956, at 4,282m. Through the first half of June, they placed camps on the Chagaran Glacier, avoiding the worst of the lower icefall by climbing the northern moraine and then threading seracs. Camp 3 was set on the west col at 6,355m after a steep ice wall. They reached the col on June 16, but took until the end of the month to move tents, fuel, and food up.

From there the route followed the exposed crest of the West Ridge, a mixed line of rock, snow and ice that required fixed ropes on the steeper sections. Brown made a key traverse around a rock cliff on the South Face. Camp 4 was placed on the ridge itself at 6,439m.

Above the high camp, the climbing continued up a narrow couloir and then mixed ground. The final technical obstacle was a short rock leaf between the two summits, graded alpine V and exposed on both sides.

On July 6, Brown and McNaught-Davis reached the western summit. The following day, Hartog and Patey, after supporting the first pair, crossed the connecting ridge and stood on the slightly higher eastern summit. Both pairs had to bivouac on the descent. Hartog suffered frostbitten toes. All four climbers reached the top.

Muztagh Tower. Photo: Hunza Adventure Tours

The French established their Base Camp at 4,496m on June 12 after approaching from the Younghusband Glacier. Their reconnaissance quickly showed the North Ridge was impossible, so they moved onto the eastern branch of the glacier.

They fixed ropes through an icefall and up a rock-and-ice spur, placing successive camps until Camp 4 stood at the foot of the summit pyramid at 6,300m. On July 6, as bad weather closed in, they spotted the British climbers moving on the upper heights.

After the two-day storm cleared, the French regained the ridge, overcame two substantial rock towers, and bivouacked high on the mountain. On July 12, Magnone, Paragot, Contamine, and Keller reached the main summit through deep snow, six days after the British first topped out. After summiting, they descended to Camp 4 after dark. Dr. Florence had waited at high camp for more than 40 hours without radio contact during the summit push.

The British party therefore made the first ascent of Muztagh Tower. The French completed an independent second ascent six days later. Both teams discovered that the mountain, while technically demanding and exposed, offered viable lines. The route, while serious, proved less relentlessly steep than Sella’s photograph had suggested.

The two expeditions were not engaged in a formal competition. They approached from opposite sides, followed separate routes, and maintained cordial relations. The British simply reached the summit first. The French, seeing the British already on top, continued their own line to completion.

Far from a bitter nationalistic race, the two teams demonstrated alpine solidarity. The French team chose the east side specifically to avoid interfering with British progress on the western side. Rather than abandoning their push in defeat after spotting the British on the summit, the French celebrated their colleagues’ historic achievement and resolutely pushed forward to fulfill their own objective. When Hartog suffered severe frostbite during his descent, the French team stepped in to provide vital assistance and support during the evacuation.

The southeast side of Muztagh Tower, showing the route. Photo: Guido Magnone for The Himalayan Journal

Since 1956, Muztagh Tower has remained one of the least visited major peaks in the Karakoram. A British team in 1984 repeated the Northwest Ridge (Mal Duff, Tony Brindle, Jon Tinker, and Sandy Allan), though they reached the slightly lower west summit rather than the true east summit. In 1990, a Swedish party consisting of Göran Kropp and Rafael Jensen also successfully scaled the Northwest Ridge.

In August 2008, Slovenian alpinists Pavle Kozjek and Dejan Miskovic made a groundbreaking alpine-style push up the steep Northeast Face. They successfully reached the upper ridge crest, but ferocious winds ended their push. Tragically, just after beginning their descent, a ridge cornice collapsed, and Kozjek fell to his death.

The 2,000m Northeast Spur of Muztagh Tower showing the line “Think Twice.” Photo: American Alpine Journal

Four years later, Russians Sergey Nilov, Dmitry Golovchenko, and Alexander Lange made the historic first ascent of the massive Northeast Spur. Their grueling 17-day climb via a new route named “Think Twice” reached the true summit, earning them the prestigious Piolets d’Or. The Russian team indicated in their expedition report that Muztagh Tower was 7,284m.

The 1956 French route has never been fully repeated to the main peak, and no further ascents of the true summit have been confirmed since the 2012 Russian expedition. Still, climbers continue to push limits here, most notably in 2019, with the first ascent of the Black Tooth (6,718m), a difficult lower spire on the mountain’s ridge.

Muztagh Tower (top left) and its Southeast Ridge, with a high point on the Black Tooth (6,719m). The solid line, with the two marked bivouac sites, is the line of ascent to Black Tooth followed by Simon Messner and Martin Sieberer in 2019. Photo: Simon Messner/American Alpine Journal

Prior to that, Kris worked as a real estate agent, interpreter, and translator in criminal law. Now based in Madrid, Spain, she was born and raised in Hungary.

#8502. Te Araroa: the boogeyman got me

Every trail has its boogeymen and its icons. On Te Araroa you run into your first of each essentially at the same time. Kilometre 135.5 marks the base of the Raetea Forest. Notorious for its mud and for being one of the first places on the trail where people end up getting heli-lifted out. At the base of the hill sits the Krishna Sanctuary, where for a donation you can camp and get fed a massive curry meal by Abhay and Jaya, the owners of the sanctuary.

I hit this on day 5, after one and a half rest days and a resupply in which I bought way too much food and also deodorant since it seems like this trail actually has showers every couple of days.

On day 5 I woke up feeling like a nervous wreck and unsure what to do with my day. I knew rain was coming the next day and was worried about the already muddy forest. I decided to just go loosely with my original plan – to get to the Krishna Sanctuary and then make a call about whether I’d climb halfway up to the Raetea summit to camp with some of my friends. That led to my first time hitching, a mere two minutes into walking, a woman pulled up in her ute with her very cute dog and loaded us into the car and drove us all the way to the Krishna sanctuary. Meeting her and being at the sanctuary was like a full reset for my nervous system. I stayed the night there on the floor of a cabin, massaged my tight calves and nursed my remaining blisters from the beach.

By the time my alarm went off at 5:15am I was feeling good. A little nervous for this boogeyman of a hill but physically strong and ready for a big push. I was so excited to be off the beach.

The day was hard, but getting up the hill went quickly, I walked with two couples I had met the night before and they were fast up and down the hills. We laughed a lot as people slipped in mud and the boys sang and did gollum impressions. By the time we reached the summit I was feeling triumphant, this hill was not so bad!! But then the rain really set in and the descent began. Steep, deep mud for 8km. Eventually I lost the couples, preferring to not rush and navigate the mud alone. I got stuck up to my mid-shins and had to dig myself out with my poles. But overall I was feeling great, my usually-a-problem knee was holding up fantastically and I had only fallen once.

Then, about 5km from the end I slipped and my left leg folded under me and bashed into some sharp roots. It was one of those falls where your whole brain sets off an alarm and you have to count to ten before you can start assessing if you’re really hurt. The sharp pain from the sicks had me wondering if my sock had ripped (luckily no) and I stood and tested my ankle – it seemed ok so I kept walking. I didn’t have much choice.

By the time I made it out of the forest, the rain was getting lighter and I meandered through a misty field trying to find the trail markers.

I was so close to the gravel road to camp when I had my third fall of the day, walking down what I thought was regular dirt but was actually extremely slippery mud, toward a gate that would let me onto the road. I fell in slow motion, swearing at the universe. This fall didn’t hurt my body so much as my ego. I threw my pack over the gate and climbed over the stile before hobbling my muddy butt up the road to the campsite.

I was so incredibly happy to see my friends and the sun peaking through the clouds. After nine and a bit hours I had made it! There was a stream for washing and collecting water and I did both, using my muddy shorts to wash both themselves and my legs. I got my tent up and airing out, and someone gave me pre-boiled water for a hot chocolate. Everything was looking up!

But what goes up must come down I guess, and my left ankle started to swell. Turns out the fall and bashing it on those sticks did hurt. I massaged it and did my best to keep off it and by morning it felt walkable, so off we set.

This day was one of emotional ups and downs, it was supposed to be the chillest, easiest day of the section. Mostly gravel roads for 23km and a dairy (convenience store) 6km in. Unfortunately, my ankle was GRUMPY.

There was a mobile voting place at the dairy so I could vote right on trail and have an ice cream at the same time! The ladies at the voting place were so kind and I told them it was the first time I was able to vote in NZ so this was a big deal for me. I cast my vote then went to the dairy and bought myself an icecream and a canned iced coffee. Glorious.

The next 10km or so up a forestry road flew by. Then my ankle decided it was once again in a bad mood. I hobbled down the forestry road to reach a stream about 1.5km out from camp and stood in its very cold waters for ages to get the swelling down. It was gorgeous and a relief.

Camp this night was much more established, with a water tank, toilet and a shelter. I decided that if my ankle was still sore in the morning I’d stay, I had plenty of food, battery charge, and I knew more people would turn up the next day.

I felt a bit sad at this prospect but I knew I’d feel stupid if I pushed it and had to get off trail. The magic of thru hiking struck this night, and we had a lovely time chatting in the shelter and eating the whole block of Whittaker’s chocolate my friend brought. I got to see a ruru (a native NZ owl) for the first time ever. We all had a good laugh when someone’s tent got raided by a possum. It’s all ups and downs.

My ankle was, indeed, still sore this morning. One of my day-one friends decided to stay with me for the day as she also had tons of food and wanted to take some time to sort out her gear and the blisters on her toes. I managed to get some messages out to Fraser and the trail angel who was going to pick me up to let them know that I was okay but delayed.

We spent the morning slowly drinking our tea and coffee, and eating breakfast. I washed some of my clothes, read with my feet up in the air to help with swelling and munched on our over-abundance of snacks. To be honest, it was exactly what I needed.

Another group of hikers turned up in the afternoon and one was a physio (the trail provides!) she assessed my ankle and did a lymphatic drainage massage on it. She was a life saver. In the morning I felt way better but decided it wasn’t smart to continue on the rougher track ahead and backtracked to the road where I was picked up by a trail angel. This is NOT how I wanted this section to go, I really was looking forward to the river sections, but I needed to be smart and recognize that even with some improvement on my ankle, it was likely an overuse injury and needed real rest and to be checked by a physio in town.

To say I was disappointed is an understatement, I have never had an issue with my ankle like that so it really blindsided me. But taking a break is not quitting. And boy will it make for a good comeback story when I’m recovered and back on trail. For now, it’s several rest days and hoping I don’t get too stir crazy.

The whole album Grace by Jeff Buckley. I had never listened to it and Fraser told me it was essential listening. I listened to it while sitting in the sun in the Krishna Sanctuary garden, I loved it.

Honourable mention: that “just keep swimming” song Dory sings in finding nemo which got me through the last 3km of the Raetea forest.

#8499. Weekend Warm-Up: First Descent Rio Cuervo

This full-length adventure documentary follows kayaker Dane Jackson and a small team down Chile’s remote and wild Rio Cuervo.

With an entire river to descend, the film wastes no time getting right into it. Dane Jackson launches into the complicated business of trip logistics, trying to find a way to get the team and their equipment to the beginning of the river. Besides him, the team consists of the trip’s mastermind, Kilian Astorga, and kayakers Tom Dolle, Eirik Hansen, Adrian Mattern, and David Sodomka.

Forty years ago, there was a road up to Lake Mayuin, the volcanic pool from with Rio Cuervo flows. It’s gone now, so they turn to helicopter transport. With their gear dangling below on a rope, the chopper carries them up into the mountain, depositing kayaks and kayakers alike on the lakeshore. They set up camp and settle in to begin the first descent of the Rio Cuervo.

The team scouts the head of the river, swelled with recent rainfall. Photo: Screenshot

The dense forest and sometimes steep banks add another layer of difficulty as they begin to make their way downstream. They have to plan ahead, as there are stretches where it is impossible to bail if the rapids become too much. This means more portaging, which is painfully slow due to the thick vegetation.

When they do hit the rapids, on-board cameras capture the frenetic energy of whitewater kayaking. But the film makes no attempt to conceal the reality of a first descent. Much of their time is spent scouting ahead by drone, poring over satellite images, portaging, and standing about debating logistics.

Sunset arrives before the end of their portage. Camping in the jungle makes for an uncomfortable night. Photo: Screenshot

Jackson and the rest of the crew soldier on, though, cracking nerdy jokes (the jungle is compared to both Dagobah and Fangorn Forest) and making the best of bad weather and rough camping. In the final few days, conditions improve, and they can spend more time on the water.

The contrast between their slow, grueling push forward and the wild speed on the river brings refreshing energy to the kayaking sections. When the river finally widens as they glide into the sea, it feels like a hard-won victory.

Early in the production of a certain musical, Broadway director Harold Prince attempted to ask Andrew Lloyd Weber what the deeper political allegory or social commentary was behind the composer’s feline opus. Weber famously took a long pause and replied: “Hal, this is just about cats.”

This movie is about kayaking. Many outdoor adventure films use the genre, and the adventure story, to explore grand themes, and some do so successfully. But when they fall flat, is it more annoying than I can begin to express. For that reason, I deeply respect the clarity of purpose evinced by Dan Jackson and First Descent Rio Cuervo.

Lou Bodenhemier holds an MA in History from the University of Limerick and a BA in Creative Writing from the University of Arizona. He’s interested in maritime and disaster history as well as criminal history, and his dissertation focused on the werewolf trials of early modern Europe. At the present moment he can most likely be found perusing records of shipboard crime and punishment during the Age of Sail, or failing that, writing historical fiction horror stories. He lives in Dublin and hates the sun.

#8496. Adventure Links of the Week

When we’re not outdoors, we get our adventure fix by exploring social media and the web. Here are some of the best adventure links we’ve discovered this week.

Lara Neumeier Makes First Female Ascent of a 5.14c: On October 7, Lara Neumeier made the first female ascent of Rhapsody (E11 7a/5.14c) at Dumbarton Rock, Scotland. She succeeded 20 years after Dave MacLeod established the route as the world’s first E11.

Neumeier’s ascent makes her the fifth woman to climb a 5.14c trad route. In an interview, she discussed the 15 climbing days and two visits spent working the route, how it compares to other routes, and her hope that the ascent will encourage more women to attempt the iconic line.

Karl Bushby, shortly after starting and now. Photo Facebook

I Left My 8-Year-Old Son Behind 28 Years Ago to Walk Around the World: After 28 years walking around the world, Karl Bushby should complete this Goliath Expedition within the next month. Now he faces an emotional homecoming: his son, whom he left behind at the age of eight, is now 36. Bushby has a grandchild he has never met, and his mother has seen him only three times since he left.

Julia Clarke hikes beside a stream in Mull, Scotland. Photo: Julia Clarke

Here are Nine British Hiking Rules Americans Need to Know: After returning to Scotland after more than a decade in Colorado, Julia Clarke realized she needed to rethink her mountain skills. She warns Americans not to underestimate the weather, terrain, or seemingly puny hills in Britain.

From wild camping rules and differences in hiking trails, to avoiding cows and brushing up on your navigational skills, she shares nine key differences American hikers should understand before tackling the British backcountry.

Women Across Diving Speak Out on Harassment: Women across the diving industry are speaking out about sexual harassment and assault. After years of raising concerns, petitioning and reporting to expedition operators and dive agencies with little outcome, many are taking to social media to share the experiences that have affected their careers as instructors, expedition leaders, and marine professionals.

Campaigners are demanding that the industry establish better and more accessible reporting systems, better safeguarding standards, and that operators vet their staff properly.

The Art of Progress: Climbing ethics are constantly evolving, and many are now reconsidering whether traditional ground-up ascents, minimal bolting, and preserving the original character of a route should take precedence over safety, accessibility, and the experience of future climbers.

Derek Franz explores this debate by looking at lines across Yosemite, Madagascar, Germany, and Patagonia, and the work underway to replace corroded bolts in many of them. The approach challenges the idea that a first ascent should remain untouched.

Three Dead After Avalanche in Chile: On October 17, an avalanche swept seven mountaineers into Laguna del Inca near Chile’s Ski Portillo resort. Three were killed and four injured.

The group was climbing toward Cerro Los Tres Hermanos when they triggered a slab avalanche. Rescue teams and the police responded within 10 minutes, and the survivors were airlifted to hospital. According to resort management, the group had entered a restricted area marked as an avalanche danger zone despite earlier warnings.

Old Traditions and New Developments on Mt. Kenya: Giovanni Trambaiolo explores Mount Kenya’s climbing history, especially the overlooked contributions of Kenyan climbers and the mountain’s deep spiritual significance to indigenous communities. He describes opening up Rainmaker, the new six-pitch trad route on the Temple Cliffs of Mount Kenya.

Three Mountain Emergencies in 14 Hours: Three hunting emergencies in northwest Colorado prompted search-and-rescue crews to respond within 14 hours, as the first significant snowfall of the season coincided with the opening of elk season on October 14 and 15.

Their first rescue call was for an overdue hunter, and the second from an individual who became separated from their group near Bears Ears and was too cold to walk. A third hunter suffered serious injuries when a tree fell on their tent as they slept. Another hunting party did not require rescue but got caught in snow, mud, and fog and spent over four hours finding their way back to camp.

Based in the UK Rebecca is a science teacher and volunteers for a number of marine charities. She enjoys open water swimming, hiking, diving, and traveling.

#8493. Grumpylocks and the Three Bears

The Ice Age Trail’s camping options are a little more restrictive than you might expect. Even the western region has plenty of segments where you can’t simply hit your miles for the day and just find the nearest flat spot. Here’s where I spent my nights on the IAT.

While some trailheads on the IAT had “No Overnight Parking/Camping” signs, the four where I stayed did not. Just four days into my hike, I camped at a trailhead next to a quiet dirt road where traffic wasn’t the reason I kept waking up. Heat, humidity, and stagnant air were the problem.

There was still no hint of a breeze by morning, and I was sweating before I left camp. I was filtering water at the next trailhead when a pair of day-hikers arrived. They parked their car, hit the trail, and it was probably half an hour before I caught up with them. They smelled nice and clean: a scent I picked up at least a minute before I saw them again. That’s how still the air was. I’m sure I smelled fine.

That morning’s trail was lined with some sort of tall grass which was shedding tiny disk-like seeds that stuck to my sweaty skin. By the time I reached the road to Haugen, my arms and legs had the texture of 60 grit sandpaper.

The three miles of blacktop between me and my intended destination were hot: probably the most uncomfortable of the entire trail. The Shady Rest Campground was about an hour away, and I was looking forward to a cool shower and a cold drink. FarOut comments even mentioned that they have air-conditioned cabins. When I arrived, the office was closed. It was a Monday.

Fortunately, one of the owner’s friends was nearby. She called the owner, who rented me a cabin. She also gave me a ride into town and some quarters for the shower. Again, I’m sure I smelled fine.

At Lona’s Corner Cafe, I sat as far as possible from the other customers. I discovered a tick on my arm during lunch. As casually and covertly as possible, I removed the tick using the array of utensils in front of me, making sure it would never bite anyone else.

After a quick stop at the grocery store for five days’ worth of food, I walked back to the campground to take a shower. Once I’d completed my chores, I literally chilled in my cabin for the rest of the afternoon.

I visited the store again on my way out of town the next morning. After breakfast on the bench across the street, I headed south on the Wild Rivers State Trail, then east on the Tuscobia State Trail. Both trails are wide (former railroads) but I was still a little surprised to be overtaken by a horse and buggy. At the end of the day, with no better options, I stopped at another trailhead.

The mosquitoes were hungry the following morning. I was carrying a small bottle of DEET for emergency use, but I wasn’t sure the situation qualified. I’d encountered worse. Still, after eight itchy miles, I wanted a break. I left the trail at the north end of Stout Road and enjoyed an hour of bug-free bliss. Even the hound that bounded beyond its house’s boundary to hound me wasn’t really a problem, despite its loud, raspy bark. It was never going to bite. It was, as they say, “All mouth and no trousers.”

I know some people hike every inch of official trail, but I need flexibility during a thru-hike. This wouldn’t be the last time I deviated from the trail, and in the end, my way was no more arbitrary than the IAT itself. The Blue Hills segments I hiked that day have since been re-routed, reducing the number of official trail miles.

This was to be my first of many days that were more road than trail. No surprise, the air was still and the mosquitoes voracious. I used some of my precious DEET to shield me while I broke camp and hiked 2.6 miles. For most of that distance, the trail crossed private land, and I could smell the cows long before I saw them. After an hour, I started a road-walk that would last all day.

At the gas station in Weyerhaeuser, I topped-up on fuel and coolant. On the other side of town, I spotted an animal that I initially thought was a large dog. I’d never seen such a lean, long-legged bear. She saw me and hurried across the road with two cubs close behind.

Eventually, the scenery started to change. Isolated farms were replaced with frequent lakeside houses. Having covered 21 miles by 1 PM, I stopped for a break at Round Lake County Park. I was way ahead of schedule, just three miles from the DCA were I intended to camp.

The IAT passes plenty of state, county, and city parks, each of which is a gift when you’re a thru-hiker. They typically have water, picnic tables, a pavilion, electrical outlets, trash cans, and pit (sometimes flush) toilets. Round Lake was my first county park on the IAT. I spent three hours at a picnic table in the pavilion, and used all the amenities. I also spoke to Paul and Cindy, the first of many hikers I’d meet who were hiking the entire IAT, one piece at a time. They offered to leave a beer for me at a local bar, and I eagerly accepted. This was a trail-magic first.

I hung out until four, went for a swim, rinsed my clothes, and wrung them out. They were almost dry by the time I arrived at The King’s Inn, two miles later. Paul and Cindy had indeed bought me a beer. I had three more with dinner, then walked one more mile to my campsite. Not a typical day, but an enjoyable one.

The morning was cool and overcast, and a light rain started at midday. A runner training for a 50k overtook me, slowing for a few minutes to chat before continuing his out-and-back. For the next 90 minutes, the rain just kept getting heavier. Eventually, on a wide section of trail, I put up my tent in “shelter” mode: footprint and rainfly only. I’d applied seam-sealant before my hike, but I discovered that the fly still leaked. The runner, Jacob, returned 45 minutes later. There was enough room in my makeshift shelter for two, even if it was a little cramped. We went our separate ways an hour after that, once the rain began to ease. It was still sprinkling when I reached my DCA an hour later, but a mylar heat-sheet beneath the leaky fly successfully redirected the drips.

Before leaving Chippewa County for Taylor County, I had a decision to make. If I spent two or three days on the IAT, I’d hike more than 40 miles of road and only half a mile of trail.

If I made my own way, I’d hike 25 miles of busy state highway and zero miles of trail. I chose option one.

I arrived in Cornell just after 9 AM, and the mayor pulled over to chat as I was walking down Main Street. After breakfast at Sam’s Place, I bought a five day resupply and hit the road at 11 o’clock. I stopped at Hidden Shady Nook campground mid-afternoon. The bartender introduced me to Spotted Cow beer, and I enjoyed a few air-conditioned hours overlooking Pike Lake.

The next day, Sunday, was even shorter. I left at 7 AM, and reached the south end of Otter Lake in less than four hours. The boat ramp was busy and the parking lot was half full. I ate some snacks while filtering water, walked a quarter mile back to the trailhead, and 0.6 trail miles to the DCA. The day was warm, with no rain in the forecast, so I didn’t bother with the rain fly. I put up my tent in the shade of an impressive tree, and settled down to read.

An hour later, although I didn’t hear anyone approach, I heard a voice say flatly, “Oh.” I raised my head just in time to see a guy turn around and leave. He was dressed more like a golfer than a hiker, and he wasn’t carrying anything. I guessed he was scouting the campsite before bringing gear and/or people.

At 4:30 PM, I had another visitor. This one wasn’t using the trail, and made no effort to hide its approach through dead leaves and dry brush. I raised my head again, and turned awkwardly to my right. An adult black bear. Realization took a second, but during that second, she continued to move deliberately, directly towards me.

“THAT’S CLOSE ENOUGH!” I was nearly at full volume.

She stopped immediately, calmly, almost casually. She avoided looking in my direction, but stayed where she was, about 20 yards away. Then, almost in unison, two furry little faces popped up out of the brush next to her. It was the cubs’ turn to take a moment. While they gathered their thoughts, I sat bolt upright. The nearest cub sprinted in my general direction.

Fortunately, the cub hadn’t been overcome by curiosity. It wasn’t helpless to resist the aroma of dried apricots coming from my bear canister. It had simply decided that, without checking for any alternatives, there was only one suitable tree in the vicinity. That tree was about 10 yards from my tent, a yard or two off the direct line of sight between me and its mother.

The sound of claws on tree-bark was surprisingly loud. Also, that little bear could climb surprisingly quickly. The second cub was close behind, just as quick, and climbed just as loudly. They went high enough that I couldn’t see or hear them.

Momma bear didn’t react when the cubs’ instincts/training kicked in. I didn’t see any change in her body language. She wasn’t aggressive, agitated, or even concerned. She just stood there, on all fours, shuffling a little from left to right, looking anywhere but at me.

They all needed some space, I decided. I narrated what I was doing as I unzipped my tent, put on my flipflops, and zipped up the door. I continued talking as I unscrewed the lid of my bear can, stuffed my toiletries into it, and screwed the lid back down. Click. Click. There wasn’t enough space in the canister for my evening meal, so I took it with me.

Armed with two blocks of ramen, I retreated down a short spur trail marked by little yellow flags. After about 20 yards, I shut the f*ck up, turned around, and waited. I was close enough to intervene if the bear went for my stuff, but far enough that the cubs would come down from the tree. That was the plan, anyway.

Momma was no longer interested in the canister, or any of my gear. It took her about 30 minutes to shuffle slowly, hesitantly to the base of the tree. She stood on her hind legs, front paws against the trunk, looking up, trying to coax the cubs down. I couldn’t see or hear any movement from above. All I could hear were Momma’s gentle calls, repeated every minute or two. Each call sounded like a sigh mixed with a groan, followed by three short exhalations through pursed lips. It was interesting, but ineffective. The cubs weren’t coming down.

By now, I’d accumulated 45 minutes’ worth of mosquito bites, and I’d run out of patience. I turned my narration back on and flipflopped back to my tent.

Breaking camp took about 15 minutes – a new personal record. I bundled everything haphazardly into my pack while giving a grumpy commentary. Mom, meanwhile, was still giving words of encouragement to the cubs.

I didn’t see the bears again, despite spending the night at the boat-ramp parking lot, only a quarter mile from the DCA as the crow flies.

This wasn’t a habituated bear, it was a food-conditioned bear. I don’t think she just happened to pick up the scent of my bear canister. With only one exception, all black bears I’ve previously encountered have been quick to show me their big jiggly ass when they ran away. This bear was brazen enough to come into camp in broad daylight, so even if she’d run away, she was probably coming back at night. The cubs did a fine job of distracting her from her mission.

I wonder how many times golfer-guy had hiked to the DCA only to find it occupied? Enough to justify a 1.2 mile round trip, apparently. Surely there can’t be that many IAT hikers using the DCA. And even if IAT hikers were always camping there, they probably know how to store their food properly. It seems likely that the DCA is frequented by non-outdoorsy types who don’t know that “A fed bear is a dead bear.”

At the very least, a fed bear is a f*cking nuisance. Its cubs might grow up to be just as much of a problem. I’m probably preaching to the choir when I tell you to store your pic-a-nic baskets properly.

I added a FarOut comment about the bear, and submitted a trail alert on the IATA website. I used a little less detail for those though.

Wisconsin road users (that snake’s fake, btw).

#8490. Couple Cycle America's New Golden Gravel Trail

Colorado couple Jules Stennes and Patch Doyle have cycled 6,124km along the newly opened Golden Gravel Trail. The Adventure Cycling Association created the route this year to celebrate its 50th anniversary.

The trail crosses eight states — Missouri, Kansas, Oklahoma, Colorado, Utah, Wyoming, Idaho, and Oregon — and stretches from Cape Girardeau on the banks of the Mississippi River to the small town of Port Orford on the edge of the Pacific Ocean.

Most of the route, roughly 70%, is unpaved. It is the organization’s longest off-road cycling trail, 1,120km longer than the Great Divide Mountain Bike Route.

The Golden Gravel Trail route. Photo: The Adventure Cycling Association

Stennes and Doyle finished in Cape Girardeau after 73 days, averaging an impressive 80km and around 12 hours of pedaling per day. “About 90% of it is mental,” they told Heartland News. “You might be tired, but you just keep on moving.”

The couple are both experienced long-distance cyclists who have previously finished Montana’s Big Sky Spectaculaire in six days and nine hours in 2022 (a self-supported 1,400km ultra-endurance race), among other bikepacking trips.

Jules Stennes and Patch Doyle during the 2022 Big Sky Spectaculaire. Photo: Bikepacking.com

Likewise, the Adventure Cycling Association suggests riders should be self-supported for the Golden Gravel Trail. Riders are advised to carry two or three days’ worth of food for the route’s most isolated sections, and up to a day’s worth of water. This is particularly important in the more arid sections, such as eastern Oregon. In Colorado, Utah, and Idaho, the trail traverses subranges of the Rockies and crosses the route’s highest point, Cumberland Pass at 3,668 m, in Colorado.

Stennes and Doyle say their journey included thunderstorms, aggressive farm dogs, and “countless hills.”

#8487. Climber Falls to Death on Ama Dablam

Search teams have found the body of Wolfgang Waschiczek, 57, of Germany, who went missing after he reached Camp 3 on his way down from the summit. Evidence shows he fell 1,700m to his death.

Waschiczek was one among over 200 climbers who lined up toward the summit of Ama Dablam this past weekend. He reached the top on October 25 with guide Sonam Sherpa, but for some reason the two of them stopped descending at a rather high point on the mountain.

“The pair decided to stay at Camp 3 overnight after borrowing a sleeping bag and other gear from other climbers,” his expedition outfitter, Real Himalaya Nepal, told The Tourism Times.

Climbers above Camp 3 on Ama Dablam. Photo: Dorjee Gyalzen Sherpa

According to the outfitter, the climbers prepared to continue down this morning. Lama asked his client to stay in place while he returned the sleeping bag to the tent where he had borrowed it. When the Sherpa returned, Waschiczek was nowhere to be found, but his crampons were still there, which suggested a freak fall. A search helicopter was called, and the remains of the climber were found this afternoon at around 4,500m.

Waschiczek is the first fatality on Ama Dablam this season.

Together with Manaslu, Ama Dablam is the most popular fall mountain in Nepal. The latest update from Nepal’s Department of Tourism on October 17 showed that over 300 foreign climbers had applied for a climbing permit. That day, the rope-fixing team opened the route to the top, and a massive summit wave started a couple of days later.

Virtually all foreign climbers are guided by one or two Sherpas, so the summit rates and numbers are remarkable. Local media estimate that over 200 climbers, among locals and foreigners, have topped out so far this season. Further teams should join them over the rest of October and November. However, no matter how tamed with ropes and anchors Ama Dablam gets, a fall from its steep slopes is usually lethal.

#8483. New Cyclone Approaches Nepal

For the second time in just over a month, a violent storm is approaching Nepal and threatening two meters of fresh snow on already overloaded mountains. This new setback comes at the height of the trekking season and also affects several climbing teams, including those engaged in alpine-style expeditions in remote areas.

The first storm hit Nepal toward the end of September and abruptly ended the climbing season on Manaslu. Worst of all, it caused an avalanche that killed 16 Base Camp staff on Himlung. The mountain remained open to commercial expeditions despite the accident, and several guided teams are currently launching their summit pushes.

Manaslu Base Camp tents buried under the snow after the September storm in Nepal. Photo: Shiddi Ghising

A low-pressure front that formed in the Bay of Bengal has now developed into a deep depression and will turn into a full cyclone tomorrow. It is expected to hit Nepal on Wednesday or Thursday through the end of the week.

The Nepal National Mountain Guides Association, in association with Senior Meteorologist Krishna Bhakta Manandhar, has put out a detailed forecast. They note that clouds spreading out from this system will hit Nepal’s mountains on October 28, especially above 6,500-7,000m in the eastern part of Nepal, including the Khumbu and Kanchenjunga regions. This will spread over the next two days, causing heavy rains throughout Nepal and snow at higher altitudes.

Authorities and local media have urged trekkers and climbers to modify their plans and avoid river areas and high passes. The main concern is for those currently in remote areas without InReach, Starlink, or satphones.

Trekkers should check with local agencies, especially those heading for the Annapurna and Manaslu regions. Several passes there were already cut or in poor condition after the previous storm and subsequent floods.

A Russian team in the Kangchenjunga region is acclimatizing to climb 7,710m Jannu. According to their latest report, they plan to touch 7,000m before attempting their main goal.

Fellow Russians attempting the West Ridge of Everest have retreated to Kathmandu to rest and recover, so they should not be affected. Andrei Vasiliev, Serguey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov, all climbing without supplemental oxygen, are enduring some lung problems. They returned to Base Camp from their second foray up the mountain last Friday, without reaching 7,500m, as they’d hoped.

After climbing in the Cholu range, Jost Kobusch of Germany and his small team moved to the Manaslu area for the second stage of his acclimatization before attempting Everest solo in winter, also without oxygen and via the West Ridge. However, the poor state of the trails after the recent floods and the approaching cyclone have thwarted his plans.

“The flood cut our planned path and, according to forecasts, the incoming cyclone will leave up to two meters of snow,” Kobusch told ExplorersWeb from Samagaon, where the team is pondering their options.

#8479. Mont Blanc Has Grown Almost Two Meters — But Not in the Way You Think

These days, topographic surveys typically show that a mountain’s altitude is decreasing due to shrinking snowcaps. But strangely, Mont Blanc, the highest peak in the Alps, has grown significantly since its latest measurement in 2023.

Mont Blanc is now 1.88 meters taller than it was three years ago, according to a recent report by France’s IGN (National Geographic Institute). The new official altitude is now 4,807.47 meters (15,772.5 feet) above sea level.

However, it may be wise to wait before changing the figure in climbing guides. Measurements are carried out every two years, and each time the registered altitude varies:

Graphic showing the results of the last few measurements on Mont Blanc, by LaChangingMeteo

Mont Blanc’s “summit is constantly shifting,” Jean des Garets, chief geometer in the Haute-Savoie department, told Le Monde.  “Each individual measurement is not significant in itself.”

So, what’s with the yearly differences? Obviously, it’s the variation in the thick but ever-changing snowcap that covers the summit.

The mountain’s rocky summit measures around 4,792m above sea level. The snow cover varies with the seasons. The difference from the previous measurement shows that 2023 was much drier at summit altitude.

The survey team on itsir way to the summit of Mont Blanc.. Photo: ING

A team from the Order of Chartered Surveyors (Ordre des géomètres-experts) acclimatized first by climbing Bishorn (4,153m). They then spent some days measuring several points around the mountain. Finally, they climbed Mont Blanc via the normal route on September 15-16.

Once on top, they pinpointed the highest point using a GNSS (Global Navigation Satellite System) pole, which measures altitude in real time.

The recent survey featured an interesting novelty. In addition to altitude, the survey also measured Mont Blanc’s gravity by installing a gravimeter on the summit for the first time ever. This measured the force with which the Earth attracts the device. In so doing, they wanted to determine whether the summit has sunk, regardless of ice cover.

The gravimeter on the summit of Mont Blanc, September 16. Photo: ING France

“When the height of Mont Blanc changes, we can’t know for sure whether the ground or the rock has moved or if the ice has melted,” explains Olivier Jamet.

Gravity provides the missing information: mass. If the ice has melted, there is less material under the instrument, but the rock has moved closer to it. Distinguishing these two effects requires a model of the ice cap and the massif, and above all, repeated measurements at the same location. And the effort is worthwhile, especially now that the effects of climate change on Alpine glaciers are becoming increasingly apparent.

The gravimeter on the top of Mont Blanc measured the gravity at 9.7944689 m/s².

“For comparison, this value is 9.81 m/s² in Marseille (located at sea level) and 9.8043046 m/s² in Saint-Gervais-Le Fayet (580m above sea level),” ING reports. “This difference in value, even if it seems small, allows for the detection of changes in mass, particularly in the mass of the ice. Repeated over time, these gravity measurements will thus contribute to improving the determination of the altitude of the highest peak in Western Europe.”

#8477. Walking and Canoeing from Kansas to the Gulf of Mexico

In April, Robert Cowden, 52, set off on foot from New Haven, Kansas, on a two-stage journey across the United States. First, he planned to walk nearly 2,000km to Pittsburgh, then canoe 3,200km downriver to the Gulf of Mexico. With him is his dog, Enzo, a pointer-mix.

Robert Cowden and Enzo. Photo: Enzo The Great: An American Expedition

When he left New Haven with Enzo, Cowden was at a low point. His battle with alcohol addiction had cost him his job, car, and home. Entering a residential treatment program would leave Enzo with no place to go. Now sober and with housing waiting for him after the end of his journey, Cowden sees his expedition as part of the larger effort to rebuild his life.

During the walking stage, Cowden towed his camping gear and supplies in a cart, which Enzo could ride in to take a break from walking. Setting out with very little, Cowden has relied on the kindness of strangers, both online and on the trail, to continue his expedition.

“The number one warning you’re going to get on a walk across America is, ‘Be careful, there’s creepy people and bad people,'” Cowden recalled, speaking to a local KOMU 8 reporter while passing through Missouri. Instead, he’s been overwhelmingly met with generosity and helpfulness.

Cowden shows the wear on his trail shoes, as Enzo looks on. Photo: Enzo The Great: An American Expedition

Cowden completed the walking stage in September. Now, he’s on the Ohio River and hopes to reach the Gulf by the end of 2026. While the second stage lets him and Enzo get off their feet, it has its own challenges. They launched the canoe into the Allegheny River at Pittsburgh. It soon joined the Ohio, and lengthy stretches of slow water pushed Cowden to paddle continuously.

It’s 1,579km down the Ohio to its confluence with the Mississippi in Illinois, which Cowden and Enzo aim to complete in under 40 days. They’re currently on pace, averaging about 20km a day.

Cowden posts regular updates on Facebook and on the expedition’s webpage.

Lou Bodenhemier holds an MA in History from the University of Limerick and a BA in Creative Writing from the University of Arizona. He’s interested in maritime and disaster history as well as criminal history, and his dissertation focused on the werewolf trials of early modern Europe. At the present moment he can most likely be found perusing records of shipboard crime and punishment during the Age of Sail, or failing that, writing historical fiction horror stories. He lives in Dublin and hates the sun.

#8476. Forester Pass, Through the Notch — John Muir Trail Day 5

A truly scary thing happened in the middle of last night.  I lay in my sleeping bag and suddenly realized I couldn’t remember the name of the highest mountain in the Lower 48.  Yes, the one I had climbed myself just two days previously.  I mean, I couldn’t think of it AT ALL.

I thought, “Ummmm… Mount McKinley, that’s in Alaska.  Mount Mansfield, that’s in Vermont.  Mount…”   I came up with Mount Whittier and I thought, “Maybe that’s it, Whittier.  Is it?”  It didn’t really sound right, but I honestly couldn’t think of the name.  I groped for it, but it just would not come to me.

Finally, I fell back to sleep and then, as I woke up, it gradually came to me.  “Oh, Whitney, yeah, Whitney, yes, Mount Whitney!”  But what was going on?  Was I getting  Alzheimer’s?  As I said, it was a very scary thing.

I also spent a couple of hours of my allotted sleeping time thinking about my sisters.  Sam urged that I find forgiveness.  I thought maybe I could write to them and say, “Look, I have a deep well of sadness and disappointment at how this has played out.  Yes, and anger too.”

“But there is also a well of forgiveness in me waiting to be awakened.  At some point in the future, in the near or far future, you may consider the possibility that you were not completely fair to your brother.  A little doubt may creep in about whether you honored your sibling relationship in a truly loving and caring way.  If that day ever comes, remember that well of forgiveness remains in my heart.”

Alas, the result of all that tossing and turning was that eight hours of sleep was actually four hours of real sleep.

Then the alarm went off, right at 4:30.  We wanted to get up early to go over Forester Pass.  At 13,153 feet elevation, it is the highest point on the Pacific Crest Trail and the highest pass on the John Muir Trail.  We wanted to get across before the weather changed.

The tendency had been for good weather in the morning and then, by late morning or early afternoon, the clouds built up, and the weather got stormy.

When the alarm went off, I felt like I hadn’t slept much at all.  Also, I was still coughing.  So I was not moving very quickly.

One brilliant move I made was to set up for breakfast in my sleeping bag.  For the first time on trail, it got cold during the night.  When I went out to pee, I thought it might be nearly morning and I moved my bear cannister close to my tent flap.

Back within the tent, I wondered whether I ought to insert my silk liner inside the sleeping bag for the first time.  I decided if it was nearly 4:30 I would not bother.  But the Garmin showed it was barely 12:30 – half past midnight!  Facing four more hours of attempted sleep in the cold I got out the silk liner.

Oh, my goodness, the sleeping bag liner makes such a difference!  It’s just wonderful, the difference between chilly and toasty.  It weighs almost nothing too; definitely one of my favorite hiking luxuries.

After the alarm, I had my “breakfast in bed.”  Then I lay in my sleeping bag for a while letting my digestion settle before going out to poop.  Less than ten minutes later I had assembled my tools and was facing the cathole I had so cleverly dug the night before.  All well there, I returned to my campsite and began to break it down and pack.

I was slow.  I don’t know why, because my pack was getting smaller with less food in it.  It should have been easier and faster.  In any case, our planned 5:30 departure turned out to be closer to 6:30, but still earlier than most of the campers in our vicinity.

We were on our way to Forester Pass.  I worried that it might actually be harder to tackle than Mount Whitney because we would cross with our full packs, not the lighter version we had carried to the summit.  As we left camp, the first thing we discovered was a sign indicating the pass was not four miles distant but five.

But it was a glorious morning, so beautiful.  Soon after our departure, the sun rose and the skies were blue; the glow shone across the mountains, across the boulder-strewn hillsides.

We cast long shadows in the early morning!

We even discovered a little early morning company!

How does Mr. Rabbit know that I am not a predator?

We ran into a guy named Marty, a carpenter from Salt Lake City.  He had decided that being a carpenter alone was not going to provide him with income in his old age.  So, he began buying dilapidated houses and fixing them up.  He then turned them into rentals.

Sam sensed the possibility of a political dispute.  He interjected diplomatically that it was time we kept moving.  Still, we walked with Marty for quite a long time as we gradually made our way up the valley, higher and higher, closer and closer to Forester Pass.

Along the way we met another hiker, Lauralyn.  She and her husband Doug own the Mt Williamson Motel and Basecamp, a lodging in Independence, CA famous among hikers in the High Sierras.  I wondered whether Sam and I might stay there a night when we got off trail.  She encouraged us.

Lauralyn seemed really nice. She was also inspirational.  She was no longer young and skinny, but her enthusiasm for hiking the High Sierra was unabated.  Her pace may have slowed, but her vigor and sunny disposition still glowed.  I really hoped we would stay at her motel, and I volunteered to recite The Raven for the owners and guests if we stayed there.

Meeting her brought home that Sam and I were just a couple of days away from going off trail at Onion Valley.  I asked her where the best steak was in the vicinity and she told us to go to The Seasons restaurant in Lone Pine.  I was salivating already.

Salivating, yes, but coughing too.  I was still coughing so much.  Blowing my nose frequently or hawking up big globs of mucus from my lungs.  It was disgusting and demoralizing.  Since starting out, I had better days and worse days, but overall, I had not felt healthy and well at all.  This respiratory infection just felt endless.

As we grew nearer, Marty pointed out a low-lying ridge that he thought was Forester Pass.  I disagreed, suggesting it might be a notch on a different ridgeline. As we got closer it became clear that it was the tiny, narrow notch.  The approach is a slow and steady uphill until the base of the mountain, when it becomes an almost vertical face.

The “notch” seen from below. If you look closely, you can see the outline of the trail passing just below the giant boulder filling the notch.

There was a stream at the base and Marty went on alone as Sam and I stopped to replenish our water.  The ascent is basically into a rock wall.  In 1930 they cut zigzag switchbacks going up the side of the cliff face.  It was a big engineering feat. At one point, a young man died in the process of making it.

Donald Downs was only 18 years old. He was a few weeks shy of his 19th birthday when he died, and his fellow workers created a plaque and left it there in his honor.

Photo courtesy of Lawrence Beck (since I forgot to capture it when I passed by)

I was amazed to have the energy to hike, especially as we began to steadily climb.  It was a little past 10:00 a.m. and our theory about “good weather in the morning” was about to take a hit.

It is astonishing, in the mountains, how fast the clouds can come in.  Suddenly, as we hiked upwards, we got pelted with graupel.  Those little pellets – neither snow nor ice — are not hard enough to be hail and not wind-driven enough to be sleet, not flaky enough to be snow, nor wet enough to be rain.  In a way, if we had to face precipitation, this was perfect because they hit us softly and then bounced off of us.  Neither of us really needed rain gear because it wasn’t accumulating on us.  On the other hand, it was not easing up either.

Not the best shot of it, but you can see the graupel landing and sitting on the plant’s leaves.

Finally, we reached the notch we had seen from afar and climbed the last rocky ascent to Forester Pass.  The moment was triumphant but short-lived, since the weather was bad and the thunder was thundering.

Sam said, “Let’s keep going,” and we did.  On the other side of the pass was a long, long, long downhill.

It began with switchbacks at first, all well above the tree line.  At that altitude the rocks are plainly visible and, as I frequently did on the trip, I asked Sam to explain the geology to me.  He studied the subject in college and made a career in it.  For my part, I am curious about everything and glad when I find a passionate expert who seems to welcome my questions.

We would look at a slab of granite, for example, and Sam would explain that granite is made of mica, quartz, and feldspar in varying proportions.  He got especially excited when we encountered crystal inclusions in the rock, which he termed phenocrysts.  In fact, I suggested that his trail name should be “Phenocryst,” though I am not sure it stuck.

When the conversation turned back to my sisters, I saw Sam get visibly annoyed for the first and only time.  He was talking about the Dalai Lama’s book, The Wisdom of Forgiveness.  In it, the Dalai Lama apparently discusses forgiving the Chinese for their atrocious behavior in overrunning Tibet.

I could not resist commenting that if there was any analogy with my sisters, then, seeing how little success the Tibetans have had in changing Chinese hearts and minds, maybe the lesson is that I should just give up on my sisters.  Sam clearly did not appreciate my flip remark.  He has such an even temper that I was astonished by his reaction and immediately apologized.

As we conversed and descended the graupel turned to snow for a little while and then to rain.  We passed some patches of snow left from the winter.

This was not the first snow we saw, but given our elevation I was surprised not to see more than we did.

We concluded the rain was not a passing shower, and I finally put on my rain poncho, and Sam donned his rain gear.

It wasn’t truly miserable, but it was not very pleasant hiking in the rain.  The next day we were going off trail at Onion Valley, where Sam’s rental car was parked, so we wanted to reach Vidette Meadow to ensure a moderate distance the following day.

As we hiked, we watched the weather changing in the mountains.  It is so unpredictable, because you cannot see what is just over the nearest ridge.  At times it felt like we were about to get clear skies, then it felt like the heavens were going to burst open in a thunderous flood.  In fact, it did neither, it just rained and rained as we descended.

Vidette Meadow was a large area with many potential campsites.  We checked out about ten of them, seeking a couple that were not too wet and soggy from the rain.  At last Sam found two fairly close together.  One was a very dicey spot right under a tree, but Sam said he wanted it.  Who was I to say no?

I took the other site which was wetter, but larger and flatter, and we set up.  It was still dripping rain when we started and then it came down a little harder while we were making camp.  So it was not terrible, but not so nice.  I was really tired.

Approving my campsite, with a little hill behind me…

It was a long day. Basically, I moved everything I owned into the tent. When the weather is nice, I leave a lot of my gear outside. But I thought, with the rain, let me just bring it all in.

I cold-soaked a beef stew, my last dinner before resupply.  Then I got ready for bed.  Sam was really cold the night before, when I used my liner, so I loaned him my puffy.  I was mostly using it for my pillow anyway, and I figured I could work out some alternative method for that with some odds and ends.

As I lay in my sleeping bag, I hoped the weather would be clear and dry the next morning.  I really didn’t want to pack out in the rain. We would go over Kearsarge Pass and back down to Onion Valley to pick up Sam’s car.

Then what?  I committed to doing this blog, even if I didn’t succeed in completing the John Muir Trail.  And I had to admit, completing the trail was in doubt.  The cough and the mucus and the endless, endless, respiratory infection were getting more-and-more debilitating.

Mount Whitney and now Forester Pass are achievements, nothing to sneeze at. But I had hoped and dreamed of the John Muir trail for at least a year.  To abandon that now would really be disappointing.

We will just have to see what happens.  Tomorrow is another day.
