#8473. Animal Attack Roundup, Oct. 27

Most victims of animal attacks around the world are not tourists but the people who live amid potentially dangerous animals all the time. Here are some incidents from the last seven days.

A tiger killed two farmers in separate incidents about five kilometers apart within 24 hours in the eastern corner of India’s Maharashtra state.

Sixty-year-old farmer Nana Kambadi was killed by a tiger while working in his field on Saturday evening. The following evening, Premila Mahadole, 40, was attacked while harvesting rice. Her body was later found in the field. Officials suspect it was the same tiger, but this has not been confirmed.

The back-to-back killings have thrown residents across the district into a panic, according to the Times of India. At this time of year, many are out in their fields harvesting rice at the edges of forests.

The death toll from human-animal conflicts in just this part of Maharashtra state has now risen to 35 in 2026, according to officials.

A family herd of wild Indian elephants. Photo: Shutterstock

An elephant killed a man who was trying to drive a herd of 23 elephants away from his village in Jharkhand state in eastern India. According to forest officials, the elephant seized Nicholas Topno, 40, with its trunk, dragged him nearly 500m, and trampled him. The herd, which included five calves, had been damaging crops in the area. Officials had been monitoring the movements for several days and warned residents not to approach. Our team has been monitoring its movement round the clock for the last five days, but some villagers still ventured close to the elephants,” forest officer Shekhar Singh told the Times of India. Bear warning sign in rural Japan. Photo: Shutterstock Japan A 93-year-old woman was attacked by a bear in her yard one evening this week in Yamanashi Prefecture west of Tokyo. She suffered facial injuries and a broken right leg but remained conscious and was able to speak when taken to hospital. She survived. Because bear attacks continue to be a problem in many parts of Japan, officials have warned residents to avoid unnecessary outings. Members of a hunting association patrol the area, and students are either bused to school or driven by their parents. A medic in the group tried to help, but she died at the scene. Officials have closed the beach. Great white shark, South Africa. In the first incident, a herder named Abubakar Aden Dube Bute was grazing his calves when he happened upon a herd of elephants. He tried to flee but failed and sustained multiple serious injuries to his head, ribs, and legs. Later, 72-year-old Abdikher Sheikh Ibrahim, originally from Somalia, died on his way home from fetching water. Another man with him escaped unharmed. A Cape buffalo in Uganda. Wildlife officials told ABC that the woman hadn’t done anything wrong. They are searching the area for the bear, which is possibly a mother with a cub.

#8469. U.S. Trio Make First Snowboard and Ski Descent of a Near-7,000'er in Langtang

American snowboarder Nick Russell and skiers Adam Fabrikant and Billy Haas have just returned from Langtang with a first snowboard and ski descent of the south face of the formidable Dorje Lhakpa (6,966m).

The team climbed the peak, often known as the Langtang Pyramid, in two days in alpine style. They summited on October 20 and rode/skied down via the same line on the south face, while American photographer Blake Gordon and Canadian cinematographer Leo Hoorn filmed from a high camp.

On the summit of Dorje Lhakpa, October 30, 2026. Photo: Nick Russell

“The south face of Dorje was always the goal, and I’d been planning/dreaming of it for over two years,” Nick Russell told ExplorersWeb while on his way to the airport.

The expedition reached base camp on October 6, shortly after an intense storm blanketed Nepal’s mountains with heavy snow. For them, however, the snow was a blessing rather than a curse.

“The cyclone gave our zone some much-needed snow down low, and on the face, it allowed a clean descent (no down climbing, no rappels),” Russell said.

Sickness slowed the beginning of the expedition. “Three out of five of us, myself included, caught COVID,” Russell said. Luckily, the climbers recovered just as the weather cleared and winds dropped, followed by a string of perfect days.

After the descent. Photo: Nick Russell/Instgram

“Adam, Billy, and I all carried our own gear, set the tracks, and climbed in alpine style on the face,” Nick Russell said. The team had hired three Sherpa climbers (Dawa Geljee Sherpa, Kami Sherpa, and Nuri Sherpa) who helped the camera crew get their gear to a high camp, plus a base camp crew, outfitted by Shangri-La Nepal Trek.

High camp at 6,000m on the south face of Dorje Lhakpa. Photo: Nick Russell/Instagram

The line of ascent/descent followed the snow from below 4,500m to Camp 1 (4,900m) by crossing an icefall. According to the team, this was the only real crux of the ascent, due to overhead serac hazard. At least, the exposed section was short — less than an hour.

On the first day of the summit push, the team continued to their high camp at 6,000m, below the col and at the base of the snowy face. Russell recalls the details of the climb as follows:

The south face is quite steep and sustained above the bergshrund, with sustained 45-50˚ and pockets of 55º, we estimate. The face had seen so much sun [over] the past two weeks that the rising conditions were the biggest unknown of the entire project.

We didn’t know whether or not it would be too icy to ride/ski until we got on the face. The snow was mostly firm, pretty much on the brink of being edge-able. It was two tool and crampon climbing the entire way, with no proper rests to take the pack off.

It took about 7.5 hours to climb the face, and we topped out around 1:30 pm. It took roughly 1.5 hours to descend, with breaks for the cameras to reset.

A climber leaves almost no tracks in the hard snow on Dorje Lhakpa. Photo: Nick Russell/Instagram

The three summiters started down from the top at the same time, Russell on snowboard and his partners on skis. It was anything but easy.

“The snow was more firm than I would have liked, but just edgeable enough to hold an edge,” Russell recalls. “Between the altitude, exposure below, steepness, and how firm it was, it was by far the heaviest line I’ve ever ridden.” He added that if the snow had been a little harder, they would have had to rappel down.

The hard snow on the upper sections. Photo: Nick Russell/Instagram

“You always hope for stable, boot-top powder, but that’s rarely the case at high altitude,” Russell explained. “Instead, you make the most of the conditions presented and try to do it as safely as possible.”

He added: “The entire line was a no-fall zone; one lost edge, and it’d be over. Regardless of conditions, it was a dream for all of us to ride off the top of a peak in Nepal.”

After a partial descent, the team spent the night at high camp, hoping to ride some interesting slopes they had spotted earlier, but finally decided to bail the next morning. “We were satisfied,” Russell said. They continued on skis/snowboard all the way down to the moraines below Camp 1 around 4,500m.

Childhood friends Fabrikant and Haas often partner up on major ski expeditions, mainly in Alaska but also in the Himalaya. They climbed and skied both Gasherbrums 1 and 2 without oxygen after climbing them in the same style in 2024, together with Brendan O’Neill.

“They are the strongest partners I’ve ever been in the mountains with,” said Russell, who has also climbed and snowboarded twice in the Indian Himalaya and twice in Nepal.

“I tried Dhaulagiri in 2022 with Blake Gordon and Dan Corn, but the difficult conditions that year coupled with the loss of Hilaree Nelson [who fell to her death while trying to ski down Manaslu] didn’t allow us to make very much progress,” Russell said.

“I’ve always dreamed of riding lines in the Himalaya, and this felt like a major step forward in my personal journey,” he concluded.

While this is the first ski and snowboard descent of Dorje Lhakpa’s south face, the legendary Marco Siffredi snowboarded the west ridge of the mountain in 1999, with Bertrand Delapierre. Siffredi perished shortly afterward on the Hornbein Couloir on Mount Everest. “Dorje Lhakpa first entered my psyche from Marco and Bertrand’s descent,” the rider recalled.

The south face of Dorje Lhakpa was only climbed for the first time in 2021, by Spaniards Mikel Inoriza, Iker Madoz, and Mikel Zabalza.

“I came across a photo of the south face and the American Alpine Journal article from the Spanish team’s first ascent in 2021,” Russell said. “The massive south face is visible from the Kathmandu Valley on a clear day, and it is honestly crazy to me that no one had skied it before.”

“Today,” he went on, “people are so hyper-focused on the 8,000m peaks (for good reason, I get it), but there are still virgin lines waiting for a snowboard/ski descent in the 6,000-7,000m range. It just takes a shit ton of work to make it happen.”

#8460. Saddle to Paddle: Bikerafting From Canada to Mexico

Pete Streufert and his friend Carter (no last name) are cycling 4,025km and packrafting 645km across the U.S. from Canada to Mexico. Starting in Glacier National Park, they will cross four rivers and six U.S. states to finish in El Paso, Texas.

Their route connects the rivers with long-distance cycling trails. This allows the pair to cross landscapes that would usually require separate trips by bike and watercraft. Streufert, a geospatial wildfire scientist and cartographer, came up with the route by combining existing GPS tracks and geographical data from Bikepacking.com, American Whitewater, and OpenStreetMap. He overlaid cycling corridors and rivers to identify where the two could connect.

Before starting the journey on September 17, he said they could find no record of anyone using this particular combination of rivers and cycling routes. So it is possible that they are the first to do so.

They started what they neatly call the Saddle to Paddle Traverse on September 17, from Glacier National Park, Montana, on the Canadian border. They kicked off the first packrafting section with a 115km descent of the North Fork of the Flathead River, which forms part of the western boundary of Glacier National Park.

From there, they followed the Great Divide Mountain Bike Route through Montana toward Jackson Lake, Wyoming, for 1,107km. Here, they hit their second paddling phase on the Snake River.

Every time they reach a river, the pair inflates their rafts, load their bicycles aboard, and paddle downstream. Then at each takeout, they deflate the rafts, attach them to their bikes, and continue riding.

After 130km along the Snake River, their route joined the SLoToJa cycling corridor. They pedaled through Idaho, Wyoming, and Utah. Here, a short connector track took them onto the newly developed Golden Gravel Trail. A further 860km of cycling brought them to Utah’s Green River.

They then paddled 328km through Desolation and Gray Canyons, including a handful of Class III rapids, and their only Class IV rapid of the trip.

Pulling their rafts out in Canyonlands National Park, they took the White Rim Trail to Moab. They are now taking a few days in Moab to “get all the mud off our bikes and escape the rain for a day or two before we keep heading south,” says Streufert.

From here, they will once again pick up the Golden Gravel Trail through the La Sal Mountains and across Colorado, then continue on the Great Divide Mountain Bike Route to New Mexico.

Paddling the Green River. Photo: Pete Streufert

A final paddling section on New Mexico’s Rio Chama will take them to the last leg of the trip, a 950km ride to El Paso.

The pair are riding Rodeo Labs Flaanimal 6.0 Steel, fitted with 29-inch Vittoria Mezcal tires, and using Kokopelli packrafts. The pair have described this as a “self-supported” route, although of course they’re replenishing their food along the way. They seem to combine camping with staying in towns.

View this post on Instagram See this post on Instagram

They should complete the journey within the next few weeks, within their two-month timeline. You can follow their progress here.

#8458. Tiorati Trials

One thing leads to another resulting in a rough day on the trail.

Six weeks into the season, and it might be over. The football season, that is. My rag-tag team of fantasy football players have been doing their best, but luck hasn’t been on my side this year. I got the big performances I needed during the Monday Night Football game, but ended up less than one point from a victory. I now find my team amongst the basement dwellers with 5 wins to 9 losses. A team that has just 7 points more than me, representing a difference under 1%, has 8 wins to 4 losses.

It shouldn’t matter, but this narrow loss took the air out the room for me this morning. It can’t be rationalized, when sports aren’t going your way, it affects your mood and often spills over into the rest of your life for a time. At least for today I’d be carrying that with me.

At least the weather was on my side, it was comfortably around 45 degrees. That made packing up a pleasant experience and I was on the trail before 8:00AM, already eager to get the day over with. At least I had a shortcut on the agenda just ahead. A trail marked by a rectangular white square with a red circle in the middle led the way over Goshen Mountain. I followed the Japanese-flag looking blazes to Tiorati Road, which runs past Lake Tiorati. Along the shore of the lake is a beach and just further up is a picnic area. After that the trail rejoins the AT by the two water towers I passed yesterday. It is a nifty shortcut. I suspect many hikers take this route as the picnic/beach area has loads of amenities for hikers; water bottle filling, swimming, restrooms, showers, and vending machines.

I was still bothered by my team’s narrow loss and hiking with disillusionment. The trail was starting to respond in kind. This section of New York is rocky to be sure. Foot placement takes concentration and constant corrections when you find that your foot isn’t as stable as you’d ideally like it to be. Rock steps are a regular presence. Then there is the route of the AT. While the trail stays low, this isn’t a mountainous area, it still climbs and drops endlessly. I found that I was rarely looking ahead, always up or down. The constant barrage of terrain was making the day unpleasant. I didn’t want to talk with any of the hikers I passed on the trail. I thought about “cancelling” this post, writing something to the effect of it being a day that I’d rather forget. My brain could only conjure up all the things I didn’t like about the trail today. That was a long list. But writing it all out would make this post really whiny. I didn’t want to insult the good people of New York by writing a long negative post. I wondered how I was going to write anything worth reading.

I rumbled along, eventually reaching the road where I rejoined the AT after getting a bit lost yesterday. This would be new territory for me. The trail climbed steeply to Buchanan Mountain. I was reaching a new low. Getting lost yesterday put me on a far easier path than going up and over the mountain, even though the route was substantially shorter. I came upon a group of hikers at an overlook who warned me to be careful on my way down the mountain. I probably should have paid the warning more mind, but I’d seen miles and miles of this type of terrain before. I navigated my way down through the rocky descent. The leaves took away any hint of what the rocks buried below might look like. My trekking poles skipped off the rocks, offering no aid. I had to rely on my feet and ankles. It went well until it didn’t. I don’t know what I stepped on, but it wasn’t flat. My left foot slipped, bending my ankle at an awkward ankle. I cursed, maybe loudly enough for the group I had passed to hear. There was no lingering effect from the event, but it didn’t help my mood at all.

Rock steps on the section of trail known as “Agony Grind”.

A bird flies near Arden Mountain over I-87.

I came to a stream right around the point where I lost the trail yesterday and stopped to filter some water. I needed to regroup and find some way to redeem the day. My only idea was to hike back to Route 5 and save myself a bit of climbing by road walking back to my van. It looked to be roughly the same distance, but considerably flatter. Just down the road I saw the Albert Wisner Public Library, which would remain open until 8:00PM. I’d feel better if I could get my blog posts for yesterday and today scheduled and reduce some of my weekend workload. I pulled on my pack, worked through the rest of my trail snack, finished up the water I had just filtered, and hiked on.

Just above Fitzgerald Falls was a large pool fed by the same creek. A sign read simply “AT SPA”. I could have done with a spa day, but given the recent overnight temperatures I think this one might not have done me a whole lot of good. In the summer though, it would have been a glorious stop.

Eventually I reached the road and turned left. About an hour later I was back at my van getting cleaned up. The library was a short 7 minute drive away, but when I walked up to the doors I found that it was closed due to flooding. I had planned on going to the grocery store afterward for some town food anyway, but I was annoyed that I’d probably end up falling behind on the blog. In the first bit of good fortune all day, the Shop Rite had a seating area where I could get my work done. Plus, it was open until midnight. I could enjoy a bit of food and then work through my write-ups before heading back to the trail. The store even had the TV in the seating area set to the World Series, so I got to watch baseball for the first time in months. It had take a while, but the day finally managed to turn a corner.

#8455. Solo Trekker Flouts Khumbu Rules, Evacuated After Cliff Fall

A 26-year-old Australian solo trekker who fell from a cliff near Lobuche in the Everest region has been evacuated by helicopter to Kathmandu. He is recovering in intensive care. By law, all foreign trekkers are supposed to have a guide in the Khumbu.

Joshua Patrick Cherubino sustained severe head injuries after falling at Kongma La Pass. He was first taken to Lobuche, then flown out on October 27, according to The Tourism Times.

Kongma La, at about 5,535m, is the highest of the trio of high passes on the classic Everest Three Passes circuit. It links the Chhukung side of the Imja Valley with Lobuche over rocky, non-glaciated moraine. The crossing is long and remote; the descent toward Lobuche is often loose underfoot and comes after hours already spent at altitude.

The case has again drawn attention to Nepal’s rules in the Khumbu. Since 2023, the Nepal Tourism Board has required that all foreign trekkers be accompanied by a licensed guide within national parks, including Sagarmatha.

In practice, the local Khumbu Pasang Lhamu Rural Municipality has continued to issue its own permits and has not strictly enforced the national guide requirement. Thus, independent trekking remains common on the main Everest routes. Officials quoted by The Tourism Times described unguided travel in the region as a violation of the mandatory rule and a source of preventable rescues.

Cherubino was traveling alone when he was found. No further details on the circumstances of the fall or his condition have been released beyond the hospital’s assessment that he is recovering.

#8452. West Ridge or Hornbein Couloir? Everest Team Prepares for Fourth Attempt

The Russian team is preparing to head up Everest’s West Ridge for a fourth time. While no easy option exists, they want to avoid the extremely exposed, difficult, and uncertain ridge route. Their only alternative is the Hornbein Couloir, which would force them to stray temporarily into Tibet.

Andrei Vasiliev, Vitaly Shipilov, and Sergey Kondrashkin are in Kathmandu recovering from a viral infection and waiting out Cyclone Arnab, which is now weakening. They will return to their base in Lobuche this weekend, determined to climb Everest without supplemental oxygen.

Everest West Ridge some days ago. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev

“So far, we have completed three rotations on the mountain,” leader Vasiliev told ExplorersWeb. “Part of this time was spent exploring different options for accessing the route.”

The Russian team has a permit to climb Everest from Nepal, as long as they attempt a route other than the standard Khumbu Icefall-South Col-Southeast Ridge. This has become the normal South Side route since Hillary and Tenzing’s first ascent in 1953.

Topo of the Russian team’s planned route on Everest, courtesy of Andrei Vasiliev

First, the Russians tried to bypass the Khumbu Icefall via the Nuptse Shoulder toward Camp 1, but heavy snow forced them to find another route. Crossing the Icefall (sharing paths with the normal route) was also too hard in the deep snow and on the shaky snow bridges over the innumerable crevasses.

“Eventually, we selected a third option, via the Lho La,” Vasiliev said. “From that pass, our planned route continues across the West Shoulder, along the West Ridge.”

At the Lho La col. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev

On their latest foray, the team reached 6,400m. “We climbed approximately twelve 60m pitches over rock, snow, and ice of moderate difficulty,” said Vasiliev.

He noted that on the way to the West Shoulder, they found traces of previous expeditions, including old ropes and snow anchors.

As for the terrain ahead of them, Vasiliev said:

From our highest point reached, the terrain ahead looks manageable. We can see two more steep rock steps, each approximately 100m high, along with possible bypasses on steep snow slopes. Beyond these obstacles, the terrain appears easier, and we hope to be able to move simultaneously.

Rocky section on the way to Everest’s West Ridge. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev

Vasiliev and his team are confident they can manage this route, despite doing so in increasingly wintry conditions.

The route linking the Lho La, the West Shoulder, and the West Ridge of Everest has been completed only twice. A Yugoslavian team led by Tone Skarja did the first complete ascent in 1979. They used the Hornbein Couloir variation on their descent.

The only repetition was done by a Bulgarian team in 1984. Hristo Prodanov reached the summit on his own and retraced his steps down the ridge but never made it back alive. Some of his partners who summited days later descended via the normal route. Three other teams who climbed the West Shoulder-West Ridge summited by traversing to the North Face, on the Chinese side, and climbing the Hornbein Couloir.

The North Face of Everest from the West Shoulder. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev

Objectively speaking, the Hornbein Couloir offers more summit (and survival) chances than the upper part of the West Ridge. However, it requires traversing into Chinese territory. The Russian team has a permit to climb only from Nepal. It is unclear if a brief border trespass could be considered, and Vasiliev has not confirmed what they will do. “First we need to complete one more rotation,” he said.

#8449. Kili Day 8 – Mweka Camp to Mweka Gate

Mon Oct 26 5.76m Climb 4 ft (that’s what my Garmin recorded) From Mweka Camp: ~10,170 (3100m) To Mweka Gate: 5400 (1640m) stay @ Summit Lodge in Arusha

It seems that it is common practice among all trekking companies to tip the porters and guides. I don’t know how other companies handle it, but Climb Kili gives us a sheet of paper with everyone’s name and position listed. We decide how much to tip and how to split it up among all the porters and guides. Some in the group had looked up the range for the total tip. We all felt like tipping at the high end of the range, and a couple hikers contributed a bit more than that. Then we all decided how to distribute our portion of the tip to each porter (some porters also had additional jobs) and guide and added everything up.

What porters carry. I didn’t know what group these porters are from, but the combination of backpack and large duffel on their heads was very common

At our final morning song/dance, we announced his much to everyone would receive. We were told this was required by KPAP (Kili Porters Assistance Program) for transparency. We didn’t carry the cash on the mountain with us – paying when we got back to the lodge – but this let everyone know what to expect before they went their separate ways.

Not being sure if anyone had recorded the enthusiasm of the morning song/dance, I put my camera on my mini tripod and video recorded it. Additionally, we all seemed to have impromptu words of thanks for the amazing job every porter and guide did in helping all of us get to the top of Kili.

Today’s trail was steep and quite muddy as we got lower in elevation. That resulted in a couple cases where our feet slippef out from under us in the mud. But it was nothing dangerous.

To limit wisdom, sections of trail were covered in rock and cement. This was actually much more common while approaching Mweka Camp.

Lots of steps on this section of trail to allow it to descend quickly

One nice thing was that the air felt like it had so much oxygen in it

I spent much of the morning talking to Herment. He says he knows many of the guides and porters on the mountain, that they are from local villages and he knows many from there. I asked about aiding hikers. He says they help around 5-10% of hikers. Most of the ones that require a lot of help were doing shorter trips, so they hadn’t acclimated as well.

At Mweka Gate, when sitting down I can feel that my thighs are a little tired. They aren’t bad, but sitting feels good.

We got certificates and medals for making it to the top and posed with them for one last group photo.

The end is near. We can see some vehicles parked ahead.

Medal for finishing (and Peppermint – my camping turtle)

Our group with our certificates saying we climbed Kili

We had a nice lunch in the village near the gate. They also had a pretty big souvenir shop that accepted cards and electronic payments. It seemed like smart business. Lots of tour groups enjoyed lunch there. I was surprised they didn’t have any Kili patches or stickers (only magnets)

James’s Saudi Arabia plans got messed up by world events, so he is now going to join Dave and Joel on their 5 day safari. I’m sure they’ll have fun continuing a few more days together.

As should be obvious to anyone reading these blog entries, I was very satisfied with Climb Kili. I can’t compare them with other trekking companies, but I felt like they took care of all our needs. The food was nutritious and plentiful – usually more than we could eat. The guides were always looking out for our safety and were willing to help in just about any way conceivable. Their knowledge of the mountain went well beyond what was necessary to just get is to the top. Maybe the trekking companies that charge substantially more provide a lot luxury. But I certainly didn’t feel like anything was missing with Climb Kill. I would gladly recommend them to anyone else considering a Kilimanjaro trek.

#8447. Photo Contest Winners Reveal Amazing Microscopic Worlds

Since 1975, Nikon’s Small World competition has featured images produced by optical microscopes, an art that usually stays in scientific papers and textbooks. But through the carefully engineered lenses of the microscope, photomicrographers sometimes capture glimpses of strikingly surreal, alien beauty. The 2026 Photomicrography Competition winners include subjects both living and mechanical, small and very small.

The fruiting bodies of a Hemitrichia slime mold remind one distinctly of Dr. Seuss. Photo: Eric Epstein/Nikon Small World

The winning image shows bubbling globules of black ink being injected onto a piece of paper by an inkjet printer. Behind the lens was 25-year-old German design student Ole Bielfeldt, whose work explores the surprising complexity of everyday objects. His process is largely DIY: Bielfeldt builds his own setups, cobbles together parts, and learns techniques online.

“I just pick somewhere to start and go for it,” Bielfeldt explained. “You’re likely going to fail at first, and that’s what makes it even more interesting.”

The experimentation and imperfection, he added, are the most interesting parts of the process and, ultimately, more important to him than achieving the highest image quality.

Ah, mice; the humble martyrs to scientific progress. A significant amount of science seems to involve cutting up mice and learning from the result. But in this sort of photography, even the strongest mouse advocate must admit that the results are visually spectacular.

Satu Paavonsalo and Dr. Sinem Karaman of the University of Helsinki took this image of a mouse’s eye while researching drug therapy. Photo: Satu Paavonsalo and Dr. Sinem Karaman/Nikon Small World

Third place went to another rodent part: a 5X-magnified image of neurons in a mouse’s brain.

Photo: Kaelin Wulf and Rachel Flannery/Nikon Small World

In defense of humanity, we were also willing to subject our own body parts to photographic investigation. The 7th-place winner came from Dr. Bruno Cisterna and Dr. Eric Vitriol at the Medical College of Georgia at Augusta University. Using confocal imaging, which involves scanning a specimen to generate optical sections, they captured human neurons at 20X magnification.

These human neurons were grown from reprogrammed skin cells. Photo: Dr. Bruno Cisterna and Dr. Eric Vitriol/Nikon Small World

I’ll end with a personal favorite of mine, John-Oliver Dum’s image of a little jumping spider, dusted with pollen. Dum, who won second place, credits a childhood bite for his fascination with spiders. The pollen was cultivated by his wife, specifically to create images like this one.

You can disagree, but I think this little guy is adorable. Photo: John-Oliver Dum

You can view the full gallery of winners and honorable mentions here. If you want to see photos of larger things, check out the winners from the Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026, Aerial Photography, 2026 Ocean Photographer of the Year, or Memorial Maria Luisa International Photo and Video competitions.

Lou Bodenhemier holds an MA in History from the University of Limerick and a BA in Creative Writing from the University of Arizona. He’s interested in maritime and disaster history as well as criminal history, and his dissertation focused on the werewolf trials of early modern Europe. At the present moment he can most likely be found perusing records of shipboard crime and punishment during the Age of Sail, or failing that, writing historical fiction horror stories. He lives in Dublin and hates the sun.

#8443. College Students Found Dead After Hiking Colorado Mountain

The two young men who set off into Colorado’s Sawatch Mountains this month were both passionate about taking the outdoors seriously. One was studying to be a wildland firefighter, while the other hoped to become a mountain guide.

But both of them were found dead Wednesday, under circumstances that remain unclear. Local authorities spent days looking for missing hikers Kaden Matsuda, 19, and Jackson Donlon, 20.

The bodies were finally discovered near West Apostle Mountain on October 28, just outside of Gunnison, Colorado.

Matsuda and Donlon, students at Colorado Mountain College in Leadville, had planned on hiking and camping near Ice Mountain, a 13,960-foot peak located about 50 miles from Gunnison.

They left for their trip on Oct. 23. College staff notified local authorities they were missing on Oct. 26, according to the Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office. The men’s families said they were both experienced hikers.

Matsuda was studying to be a wildland firefighter, and Donlon was training to become a mountain guide.

Kaden Matsuda, left, and Jackson Donlon. Supplied: Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office

Kaden Matsuda, left, and Jackson Donlon. Supplied: Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office

Search-and-rescue teams were deployed and found their vehicle at the trailhead. Weather conditions looked risky, with heavy snow falling in Chaffee County.

“Ice Mountain is a very technical climb, and it is recommended that hikers be very experienced when trying to tackle it. That is when it is dry. Although there was only about eight inches of snow around Kaden’s vehicle and in the lower basin, Ice Mountain received one to two feet of snow,” the sheriff’s office said in a Facebook post.

Multiple local SAR teams worked on the case. Photo: Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office

Multiple local SAR teams worked on the case. Photo: Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office

Rescue teams used drones, helicopters, and dogs to search for the two hikers. On October 27, they located their tent, which had collapsed under the weight of the snow, near West Apostle Mountain (13,597 feet). Inside were sleeping bags, stoves, and other equipment, but the two men were nowhere to be found.

The next day, authorities announced they had found their bodies in the mountain’s basin. Officials declined to share potential causes of death, beyond stating that they did not suspect foul play.

The Sawatch Range of the Rocky Mountains is home to many 13,000- and 14,000-foot peaks. Some of them, like West Apostle Mountain, require technical climbing ability and become substantially more difficult and dangerous during wet weather. The route up the mountain requires traversing fields of loose boulder scree and talus that can be hazardous after snow.

From 2010 to 2017, eight people have died in the Sawatch Mountains. Falls are the most common cause of fatalities for those tackling Colorado’s 13ers and 14ers, as the state’s highest mountains are known to locals.

#8442. The 101 Best Tips for Hunting the Whitetail Rut

Published Oct 25, 2026 10:23 AM EDT

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

It’s the biggest lesson I’ve learned in more than 30 years of studying and hunting whitetail deer across North America: Don’t overthink it. You don’t need a grand plan to kill a buck, especially when the rut is on in November. Just go out and have fun, hunt every hour that you can, and use these time-proven pointers to your advantage. I’ve hunted the whitetail rut for decades all around the country for my show (BigDeerTV) and for various articles and writing assignments. Below are the best hunting tips I’ve learned and developed through the years.

1) Check the record books, and you’ll see that more giant bucks have been shot November 7 to 12 than any other days. Make sure to plan some all-day sits during this window.

2) A bunch of antler-mangled saplings or cedar branches are sign of an aggressive buck—the kind of beast you want to hunt because he’s apt to move in daylight.

3) “In many areas, the first scrapes pop up in old logging roads, slip along and scout those first.” – Jim Crumley, Virginia bowhunter and creator of Trebark camouflage.

4) “Big trees with scarring from years of rubbing are signposts. Our observations suggest older bucks deposit pheromones on these rubs, and that plays an important role in the dominance ladder of a herd. All deer, does and bucks, interact with signposts—they smell and rub them—but only mature bucks make them. They act as communal scent wicks and are located in areas with high deer traffic.” –Dr. Grant Woods, Missouri biologist and hunter

5) November 10 a few years ago, Illinois: The wind was blowing 20 miles per hour. “I wasn’t going out,” says bowhunter Gary Sulcer, “but I did.” He’d been in the woods only minutes when a doe tipped by with a bruiser on her heels. Gary’s arrow was true; the main-frame, 8-pointer scored 160. Lesson: You only have so many days to hunt the rut, go when you can, no matter the conditions.

6) “We didn’t have any trail camera photos of that buck, and I had never seen him,” says Gary Sulcer. “But I knew there was a big one in the area, he was rubbing trees as big around as your thigh.”

7) Killer bow setup: Tree stand on an edge where pines or cedars meet hardwoods. Bucks rub, scrape, and prowl for does on these break lines.

8) Best scrapes to watch: In brushy cover with doe trails nearby.

9) Watch active scrapes 50 to 75 yards from dense bedding cover. You might catch a mature buck milling around scrapes closest to his sanctuary at first or last light.

10) In hill country, look for scrapes dug 70 yards or so below a brushy hilltop. Bucks like to bed on a ridge or bench, watching for does and scent-checking scrapes below.

11) University of Georgia research: Multiple bucks hit one set of scrapes while other scrapes 100 yards away go dormant. Scout, move to, and hunt the hottest sign.

12) Set up too close to scrapes, and deer will see, smell, or sense your presence. Back off 100 yards or so, even when bowhunting, and watch for a buck circling into scrapes.

13) Wear rubber gloves and clip a mangled licking branch (which holds the forehead and saliva scent of several bucks and does) from atop an active scrape and wire it over a mock scrape near your stand.

14) Best rut stand #2: Downwind of the “X” where two trampled doe trails cross.

15) “Set tree stands between 17 and 20 feet. When a buck comes by at 20 to 30 yards, you’ll see plenty of lungs, the perfect shooting angle.” – Terry Drury, Midwest bowhunter and outdoor TV personality.

16) Best rut stand #3: Thirty yards back in the woods off the corner of a field, along a main trail. Does will come from several directions, converge in the corner, and make their way back into the timber. Bucks prowl a corner where they can see and scent-check many does.

17) In Indiana one November, bowhunter Brent Ireland got a single cam picture of a double-drop giant. He hung a stand on the ridge near his camera and killed the 199-inch buck two days later. Lesson: Get one image of a monster on his feet in daylight, move in, and hunt him.

18) Set trail cameras on different sets of scrapes, and you’ll get images of most of the bucks on your land, both the locals and the passers-through.

19) A doe that flits around with her tail erect is ready to breed or almost ready. A buck or bucks will be close.

20) Best rut stand #4: Hogback ridge flanked by crops and CRP, swamp or similar thick cover on the other side.

21) One humid Texas morning, we rattled up 15 bucks. Guide Clay told me, “With moisture thick in the air, horns have a high-pitched tinkling, bucks like that.”

22) Science out of Texas: Halloween to Nov. 8 and Thanksgiving to Dec. 8 are the best times to rattle up mature bucks.

23) Rattling bags and boxes work, but nothing beats the real thing. A solid set of 140-inch antlers are the bomb, with just the right tone and volume.

Read Next: How to Rattle in a Buck, a Science-Based Guide to Rattling Tactics

24) After rattling at a buck a good ways off, don’t let your guard down, even if he shows little interest. Sometimes a buck will walk 50 more yards, get curious and circle back to check you out.

25) Best time to rattle: Sunrise to 10 a.m. I don’t carry horns in the afternoon.

26) Hold one rattling antler tight to your body and bang and grind on it with the other antler to cut down on hand movement.

27) “If your arms and hands aren’t tired after a rattling sequence, you’re not doing it hard enough.” – Texas rattling expert Gary Roberson

28) Screw a rubber-coated hook ($2 at Home Depot) into a tree close to your stand. Hang rattling horns within easy reach.

29) A shooter trots by 100 yards out—try a quick burst of rattling to stop him.

30) Research from Texas shows ground rattlers don’t see half the bucks that come in. Elevate and rattle from high ground, or a tree stand or tripod, to spot more bucks.

31) Best-sounding grunt call for my money: Ridge Runner from Quaker Boy.

32) When a buck hears your rattles or grunts and is interested, he begins to hunt you. Set up with thick cover to your sides and behind you. Make a buck commit close as he searches for the “deer” he hears.

33) A stud chasing or tending a doe makes loud, weird sounds. Blow “urrrp, urrrp” or “urrrg, urrrg” on your grunter to mimic it.

34) Blowing a sequence of 10 to 12 grunts on your call is most realistic.

35) When a buck rolls in out of nowhere, don’t reach for your call. Bleat or grunt loudly with your voice—”baaahhh” or “eckkkkk”—he’ll stop.

36) Remember to draw your bow or aim your muzzleloader before you grunt or bleat to stop a buck. Obvious, but it’s easy to forget when a big-racked bruiser is close!

37) “The grunt-snort-wheeze is the most aggressive rut call. It can bring in a dominant deer, but it can also scare off young bucks.”—Georgia biologist Dr. Karl Miller

38) Good rattling/grunting setup: Wind in your face and rock bluff or stream at your back. A buck can’t circle downwind and bust you.

39) A deer’s eyes are oriented to pick up predator movement on or just below the horizon. You can get away with a bit more movement in a tree stand, but still, be careful.

40) Favorite muzzleloader setup: Sitting on a hillside, looking across to an adjacent hillside where I can cover 2 or 3 thickets. Bucks move all day from one cover to the next checking for does.

41) Best rut stand #5: A creek or shallow river crossing pocked with fresh tracks in brushy woods. The waterway dictates and funnels most all deer movement through the area.

42) Deep, splayed tracks 2.5 to 3.5 inches long in the mud were likely made by a buck, though the size of his rack is anybody’s guess.

43) Position a stand or blind so the sun rises or sets behind you. You’ll have an extra 10 minutes of shooting light at dawn and dusk. To hide better overall, understand deer vision and what colors deer can see.

44) “On land that has been managed for years, 5- and 6-year-old bucks can’t compete with the aggressive 3- and 4-year-olds anymore, or don’t want to. Some old giants travel across the fences and take up residence where there’s less competition for does. If that happens to be where you hunt, great.” –Iowa bowhunter Don Kisky

45) Best tip for hunting public land: Hang a tree stand in thick, secluded cover and sit in it all day. You might catch a buck rutting a doe on natural movement, or another hunter might inadvertently drive a 10-pointer to you. Either way, you win.

46) Multi-year data from a property in South Carolina showed that 95 percent of the 3.5-year-old and older bucks harvested were killed within 100 yards of a well-defined sanctuary, such as a pine stand, brushy clear-cut, or cedar thicket.

47) Around Nov. 10, break out the hot-doe scent like Tink’s #69.

48) Reach up and hang scent wicks 6 feet or higher so the wind and thermals swirl and carry the scent.

49) Texas study: Bucks split time equally at scrapes juiced with doe or buck urine. Might as well dump both into a real or mock scrape you’re watching.

50) “The weekend of Nov. 8 to 10 should be excellent this year, especially if it’s cool. I think your best shot to see a mature buck is 1 p.m. to 5 p.m. Hunt your best food source.” – Mark Drury, Iowa expert and TV personality

51) Douse a doe decoy with estrus scent and set her in a clearing where a buck can see her and approach comfortably from downwind.

52) In an abundance of caution to prevent the spread of chronic wasting disease, 12 states prohibit the use of natural deer urine and permit only synthetic scents. Check your regulations. Don’t worry, synthetics smell like deer and work fine.

53) Cut tarsal glands off a doe or buck your buddy shot, and hang them near your stand both as an attractant and cover scent. Black hocks from a buck that has rutted for weeks reek the best.

54) Did you know? You can store deer hocks in a bag in the freezer and use them again next November.

55) Watch a doe trail trodden to dirt or mud long enough, and a good buck will prowl by.

56) When a big rutting buck comes in, focus on what you need to do to execute a good shot, not how big the deer is. Read more about how to effectively shoot a big buck and avoid buck fever.

57) If 10 hours on stand are too much, sleep in, sneak to your spot at 9 a.m., and hunt out the rest of the day. A North Carolina State University study found that during a full moon, deer don’t move much in the morning, but the midday hours and early afternoon are good.

58) Good post for a mid- to late-November afternoon: 70 to 100 yards back in timber and along the thickest, nastiest ditch that leads out to crops.

59) Don’t waste precious rut-hunting time. If you sit in a spot for three days but don’t see much, move.

60) Dilemma: Pass or shoot the first buck that chases a doe past your stand because a bigger buck might be coming? Advice: If you’re happy with the first rack, take him.

61) Studies of GPS-collared deer from Maryland to Texas show that most all bucks make “doe excursions” out of their core area during peak rut. Some bucks might wander 5 to 8 miles or more, while others move 2 miles or less.

62) Oklahoma study: When bucks embark on doe excursions, they move in linear patterns. By traveling for miles in straight lines, they maximize their chances of contacting hot does. Set several stands along a linear creek bottom or ridge to intercept a buck.

63) When gun season opens, monitor where people park their trucks and enter the woods. Hunt a secluded spot that others overlook. It might be 2 miles deep in the woods, or 200 yards off a back road.

64) You’re still-hunting and a doe jumps out of a ditch. Find the nearest rest and ready your rifle, a buck is apt to roll up out of there next.

65) Wyoming, Nov. 18 a few years ago: It was 70 degrees and windy, and bucks rutted all day. I shot a 150-incher dogging a doe at 3 p.m. Lesson: Hunt hard, the pull of peak rut overrides the weather.

66) If you plan to hunt afternoons after work this season, do it Nov. 19 to 24. North Carolina State University researchers found that deer movement can be excellent the last hour of daylight during the last-quarter phase of the moon.

67) Post-rut hunting is better than you think! Research from Maryland shows that 20 to 40 percent of mature bucks continue to make doe excursions into December. Keep grinding until you get one.

68) One December in Kansas, my friend Jim Riley saw three bucks hassling a small doe. The next day he went back and saw five bucks dogging her, and he shot the biggest 8-pointer. Lesson: Find the last hot doe and stick with her.

69) Killer gun stand: Narrow weed strip between two blocks of woods. Bucks run the “point-to-point” for does.

70) First week of December, lay a doe-in-heat trail into your stand. It can actually work better now to bring in a buck because there are fewer receptive does misting the woods.

71) Studies of hunter behavior consistently show that most people hunt only a half-mile or so from a road, field or another easy area. For more elbow room and fun, hike deeper.

72) Aging a buck before peak rut: Check stomach girth; the older a buck gets, the bigger his belly gets. If his stomach sags lower than the bottom of his brisket, the buck is 4.5 years old or older.

72) Aging a buck after peak rut: Forget girth because a buck can lose 25 percent of his body weight chasing and breeding does. Glass a buck’s tarsal glands. As a buck matures, his hocks appear bigger and blacker.

74) A ditch on a ridge; a fence corner 20 yards back in the woods off a bean field; a tiny creek bend or crossing… Little “inner terrains” funnel the movements of bucks as they prowl from one doe unit to the next. Hang a stand downwind of one.

75) Expert bowhunter Kevin Robinson kills big deer in the suburbs of Missoula, Montana, but never in October. “Not hunting early for four or five weeks is hard to do, but I know how good the hunting will be as the rut comes on,” Kevin says. In November, Kevin sets tree stands low in mountain draws, often fairly close to houses, roads, and developments. “Bucks that live up in the hills start moving down and looking for does, and it’s game on.”

76) When bowhunting, always pack an extra release in your backpack (you’ll thank me later). – Alex Robinson

77) Deer are most likely to “jump the string” at 30 to 35 yards. Hold slightly lower when shooting deer at these ranges. —A.R.

78) Keep shooting your bow through the entire hunting season. During the late-season, when the temps are frigid and you’re wearing an extra layer or two of clothes, it makes sense to turn down your draw weight a bit. Just be sure to re-zero. —A.R.

79) If you’re going to bump deer while hanging a new set, follow Mike Hunsucker’s tip and use a four-wheeler and other loud equipment to make the disturbance. Deer will likely not blow out of the area when they hear loud equipment. —A.R.

80) Always wear a safety harness in your treestand. But even better, pair it with a lifeline so you are always strapped in. Most treestand accidents occur when hunters are getting into or out of the stand. —A.R.

81) Upgrade that old riflescope for better shooting at first and last light. There are now a ton of great and affordable riflescopes for deer hunters that offer much better performance than grandaddy’s old scope. —A.R.

82) Days with consistent wind (direction and speed) give the hunter the advantage. Shifting and variable winds give the deer the advantage. —A.R.

83) Don’t get hung up on “the best caliber for deer”. Bullet selection and shot placement are far more important than the cartridge you decide to shoot. —A.R.

84) When hunting public land, your first job is to get away from all other hunters. This could mean trekking deep into the backcountry or finding an overlooked spot near the road. Regardless, find the place where other hunters aren’t and you’ll find deer. —A.R.

85) If you hunt from a box blind, you should make sure to have a good shooting bag. Long range competition shooters use them religiously. You should too, because they will help make 100- and 200-yard shots easy. —A.R.

86) Once you hit that target buck, watch how he reacts. Carefully track his path of escape and his body language. Use an digital mapping app to mark the last place you saw him. Then, wait. That advice your grandpa gave you about waiting one hour before going to look for blood is still true today. —A.R.

87) If the blood trail doesn’t look good, consider calling in a tracking dog. This new, free app pairs hunters with tracking dog owners. —A.R.

88) During the lockdown phase of the rut, consider hunting where you can see into old overgrown fields. Deer feel protected in this kind of cover, but hunters can still see them moving through it. —A.R.

89) Don’t fight the heavy acorn crop (if there is one in your area). Just get in the woods with the deer and hunt the acorns. —A.R.

90) If you’re going to hang a stand in a bedding area, consider doing it at night when you know the deer are out feeding and chasing. Just be careful hanging that stand in the dark. —A.R.

91) Don’t get discouraged by “nocturnal bucks”. Expert deer hunters agree that even that “nocturnal buck” will be moving somewhere during daylight hours. You just have to find out where. —A.R.

92) A good way to hunt a nocturnal buck is to try to back track him from the area you got trail camera photos of him at night. Move cameras around to likely bedding areas (thick cover) until you are able to capture daytime photos of him (or see him from your stand during the day). —A.R.

93) Some of the best deer shooting advice came from my dad, a lifelong Northwoods hunter. It goes something like this: “Keep shooting until the buck is down or you can’t see him anymore.” —A.R.

94) Always keep your scope dialed to the lowest power during the rut. It’s possible that buck could come charging in at 25 yards, and if you have your scope dialed to 12X, it will be difficult to get on him quickly. —A.R.

95) Everyone likes to talk about accessing a stand without bumping deer, but few people actually do it. That’s because it takes real effort to figure out how (and when) to get into setups without spooking deer. But, it’s worth the effort. —A.R.

96) Cellular trail cameras are worth their weight in gold. Upgrade your cams if they are legal in your area, you might be surprised how affordable the new cell cams are. —A.R.

97) Listen carefully and that approaching buck will give himself away. Rutting bucks have a marching cadence that sounds different than a doe or squirrel. Once you hear it, turn toward that direction and get ready. —A.R.

98) Visualize the different buck-approach scenarios that could play out. Think about how you’ll react during each scenario. Think of specific details (like how you’ll move your feet). And listen to archery coach John Dudley on other ways to beat buck fever. —A.R.

99) Remember that big bucks like to search for does while walking into the wind. We all want to hunt downwind, but sometimes hunting a steady cross wind is more productive. —A.R.

100) Don’t overthink moon phases or barometric pressure or even weather. If you have a day to hunt during the heat of the rut, just go hunting. —A.R.

101) Keep deer hunting fun. When it seems like every one of your hunting buddies has tagged out and every social media influencer has killed a booner, just remember you get to keep hunting while they’re at home posting online. Every day in the woods is a good one (as long as you have the right perspective). —A.R.
